bible.title: Saal Bhar (साल भर, All Year). Why: one household's year held together by a wall calendar; plain Hindi that reads the same in Hinglish; marks no gender; puts no year on screen (rule 2); it was already the options file's candidate (options Q10). How it was checked: three web searches on 25 Oct 2026 (film, series, show or app called "Saal Bhar", then Google Play and the App Store) found nothing by that name, only unrelated titles such as "Saala". The search runs on a US index, so four checks are still to do: the Play Store's and App Store's own search, the Indian trademark register, and regional film titles. It is the title of the First take inside Retake, not the app's name. Bible: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-priyanshu-Sex-Ed/f50ea7ee-0855-46a2-8572-0aa08df5b855/scratchpad/blend/bible.md
household: Nani (नानी), turning 80, Mummy's mother. She lives in her own town and runs everything from where she sits, even a ward bed. Speaks in short orders, counts heads, warm but never a pet name: "Everyone comes." Asks chapter 2. Her object is a cane with a rubber foot. She is the elder turning eighty, and the player calls her Nani, which granddaughters and grandsons both say. It replaces Ammaji, because the player is now a grandchild, and it avoids Dadi from the rejected story.

Mummy (मम्मी), 52, your mother. She runs the family's electrical shop on the station road, facing the platform. Speaks in lists, times and prices: "Saturday, nine. Shutter up." Asks chapter 3. Her object is the shop key ring with a plain brass tag. She replaces the blend's Lalita.

Papa (पापा), 56, your father. He books every train months early. Exact and dry: "Not 9:45. 9:40." Asks chapter 1. His object is a travel list in a clear plastic sleeve, painted blank. He replaces Rakesh.

Mama ji (मामा जी), 47, Mummy's younger brother. He lives in a city, and his daughter marries from Nani's house in December. Fast, generous, worried: "Sixty guests? Make it seventy." Asks chapter 5. His object is a big black umbrella. He is added because five askers are needed while rulebook Q11 is open. His tag reads "Mama ji, Mummy's brother", since "Mama" can read as "mother" in English (rule 65).

Tinku (टिंकू), 21, your younger sister. She keeps score of everything and is the lane team's scorer. Teasing and quick, she says तुम: "Six balls, six runs. Your call." Asks chapter 4. Her object is the scorebook, shut, with a plain cover. The blend made her "never on time", which is a comic quirk, and an asker is never the comic one (rule 37), so her quirk changes.

All five: they are never on a card, never the comic one, and never the one doing the wrong in a hard topic (rule 27). They have no first names on screen, so the household marks no community. Askers are 3 women and 2 men (rule 37). While rulebook Q11 is open, each speaks in one chapter only, plus the opening and the album.

How they appear (rule 33, options Q11): each has one present-day portrait, painted from reference pictures, used as the face chip on every bubble and every card note they carry. They are face-on only in the present-day opening and album. Inside a chapter's look they are seen from behind, at a distance, or speak from off the panel with a name tag, and their object stands in for them. Ch1 Lugdi: Papa from behind in the coach doorway. Ch2 Rukavat: Nani from behind the bed's head, or through the ward door. Ch3 Station: Mummy from behind at the half-raised shutter. Ch4 Cricket: Tinku from behind on the scorer's chair. Ch5 Jadugar: Mama ji from behind at the gate under the tent lights. Household hands never reach towards the player, so no hand is ever read as the player's. Portraits have plain clothes with no bindi, sindoor, cap, turban or cross, and every face is checked close up for painted dots and lightened skin.

Five chapter voices (new). They exist because rule 22 wants each chapter's remarks from a woman and a man, while rulebook Q11 allows only one household voice a chapter. Each is met in one chapter only, never on a card, painted face-on in that chapter's look and tagged on every bubble, and they balance the talking cast at 5 women and 5 men. Ch1: Mausi, Mummy's elder sister, about 55, who talks over everyone. Ch2: Mausa ji, her husband, about 58, slow and kind. Ch3: Masterji, the tailor next door, about 60, with a view on everyone. Ch4: Captain sahab, the lane's old club cricketer, about 65, with a coach's verdicts. Ch5: Mami, Mama ji's wife and the bride's mother, about 45, practical and sharp. If rulebook Q11 is answered yes, they go.
bible.player: The grown-up child of the house, aged 22 to 30, the one everyone calls (owner answer 2, rule 8). No name, no face, no hands, no shadow (rule 7): people look out of the panel at you and hold things out towards you. You are addressed only as "you" (तुम from family, आप in the game's own voice) or by the job, "in charge" (इंचार्ज). Never bhaiya, didi or beta, and until rulebook Q7 is answered elders use no family word for you at all. You call people Nani, Mummy, Papa, Mama ji and Tinku, and in one chapter each Mausi, Mausa ji, Masterji, Captain sahab and Mami. Daughters and sons say all of these. You have two or three "You" bubbles a chapter. Each is one tap, the same whatever you will pick, never a choice, never measured, never naming a card person and never agreeing with a remark (rule 38). The tail runs off the bottom edge, the tag reads "You" | "आप", and the bubble is never yellow. After a pick your reply names only the job ("Berths, sorted"), waiting on options Q14. Hindi forms that mark no gender (rule 66; the checker flags and a native reader clears): to elders, polite commands (लिस्ट दिखाइए, चलिए, पेन दीजिए, आप आराम कीजिए, नानी); to Tinku, -ओ commands (स्कोर बताओ); offers in the subjunctive (मैं देखूँ?); impersonal हो जाएगा. Never मैं कर लूँगा/लूँगी, आ गया/गई or थका/थकी हूँ. Lines said to you are commands (सुनो, देखो, चुनो), "who should" asks in the subjunctive (कौन जाए?, never कौन जाएगा?), and sentences where you are not the doer (आज इंचार्ज तुम हो। फ़ैसला तुम्हारा। सब तुम्हें ही फ़ोन करते हैं।).

chapters.event: The week nobody circled (वो हफ़्ता जिस पर गोला नहीं था). In July the monsoon floods the family's electrical shop on the station road, and it must open again by Saturday, the busiest day. Mummy hires hands for the week from those who answered her notice. Card notes are the applicants' slips on her counter.

chapters.event: Sixty guests, one lane (साठ मेहमान, एक गली). In December, Mama ji's daughter marries from Nani's house. Sixty guests sleep in one lane, in rooms the neighbours lend; there are advances to pay, keys to hold and a gift register to keep, and Nani's eightieth cake waits for the last night. Logistics only: no ritual, dress or prayer on screen (rule 3). The bride and groom are never drawn, named or put on cards. Card notes are lines on Mami's job list.

It is their own past, not this wedding's (rule 27), and it never reaches a panel (rule 26). The blend's version, this wedding's groom's side asking for a scooter, breaks rules 26 and 27 and waits on options Q3. D7, twin C second half, matters, Believe: Saturday 6 pm, the band says it was paid only half, so whose account. Set B. Pair Dolly and Gopal. Nudge on the woman: "I paid them myself, at noon." Fixed.
D8, twin D second half, plain, Rank 2 places: Saturday 10 pm, the last night, the 2 who carry Nani's cake out. Set A. Pair Mitali and Tapan. Nudge on the man. Target 2.

Kinds: Believe (first met in its home world, Jadugar), Spend checks, Pick one and Rank, so all seven kinds are met across the take. The hard twin's first half is at D2. Over the take, the first-half nudge falls on the woman in 10 of 20 twins: the hard twins 3 to 2 and the matters twins 2 to 3.
chapters.links: Opens on the red December circle and Mama ji's card. Fixed ending: the cake comes out under the tent lights, with Nani seen from behind and the world's cloth falling. Then a tap opens the present-day album: Nani, face-on at last, says "Eighty. Everyone came." | "अस्सी। सब आए।" Next comes "Here's who you trusted with what", then the five private reading cards as built. You: "Next year. Same calendar." The Next take opens on next year's calendar with the same household and a new circle (rule 52).

bible.opening: It is present day, with at most 80 counted words in each language and at most two people a panel (rule 47). (1) Early January, your phone on a bedside table shows one message from Nani on a painted blank screen: "My eightieth. May. Everyone comes." [WAITS rulebook Q9; if the answer is no, Mummy reads it out from her own phone.] (2) In the kitchen, a free calendar from the shop goes up on the wall: a plain mountain picture over a grid of empty boxes, with months and dates as live text. No New Year celebration is shown (rule 48). (3) The household on one screen: five present-day portraits labelled "Nani, Mummy's mother", "Mummy", "Papa", "Mama ji, Mummy's brother" and "Tinku, the youngest", with quirks drawn rather than written (rule 9). (4) Mummy circles dates in red: May (Papa: "Trains: booked."), 15 August (Tinku: "Lane cup. I'm scoring.") and December (Mama ji on a painted blank phone: "My daughter's wedding. Everyone comes."). (5) Everyone looks out at you, and Mummy holds out the red pen: "And the rest? Everyone calls you anyway." | "बाक़ी? सब तुम्हें ही फ़ोन करते हैं।" You: "पेन दीजिए।" (6) Narration over one empty July week: "Some weeks nobody circles." | "कुछ हफ़्तों पर कोई गोला नहीं लगाता।" The calendar is the progress object: five circles each fill with a small picture (a berth, a cane, a shutter, a stump, an envelope). The three planned ones are red; the ward and the flood week are drawn in later in pencil, so they differ by shape and line as well as colour (rule 50). The chain runs one into the next. Ch1, the May train, ends on the wet back step. Ch2, the ward that same night, ends with Nani home: "No party. When everyone comes again." Ch3, the July flood at the shop, ends on the drain the flood cracked between two lanes. Ch4, the 15 August lane cup decides who mends it, and both lanes mend it, then Mama ji's wedding card arrives. Ch5, the December wedding, ends on Nani's eightieth cake on the last night, then the album and the reading. Every chapter follows the shared strip from the scroll design and the judges' fixes. It starts with a title card naming the hard topic's setting. The asker then hands over a list of 2 targets in card-number words. Next comes a circle page of names only over a people-free place. Each scene has one lead-in with the clock and the place, and each stop has a people-free painting behind the cards. After a pick, a settled plate shows no names, and an "it happened" panel, the same for every pick, comes only at a change of place. The chapter closes on the event painting with the stamp in the world's big moment, the list stamped, one warm reaction from the asker, your fixed reply and the fixed ending. Writers mark each rule break [BREAKS rule N: why] and each beat waiting on an answer [WAITS Q], and never fix one silently.
open_for_owner: Rulebook Q3: one hard topic in the home chapter (the ward night) or two, as you decided on 22 Oct with dowry second? The bible writes one and marks it [BREAKS rules 25 and 50]. Dowry sits in the wedding chapter instead, and a care fact is ready if you say two.

Rulebook Q11: may the household speak in every chapter? Until you say, each member speaks in one chapter only, so the bible adds five one-chapter voices (Mausi, Mausa ji, Masterji, Captain sahab, Mami) to meet rule 22's woman's and man's remarks in every chapter. Yes removes them.

Options Q11: how the household appears inside each chapter's look. Written here: from behind or off the panel, with their present-day face chip on every bubble and their object in the picture, while the one-chapter voice is painted face-on. The other two ways: today's style in every chapter, or painted in every look.
Rulebook Q9: may chapter 1 open on your own phone with Nani's message? If not, Mummy reads it from hers.

Options Q3: may a hard topic touch the family's own? The blend had Nani's own child asking for a share of her house, and this wedding's groom's side asking for a scooter. Both are moved to other people's own cases (a neighbour's quarrel, a relative's past refusal).
Rulebook Q5 and options Q15: may the end of a chapter say how the event went ("At Nani's door: 6:30", "Lost by 4"), when today nothing between chapters may look like a score?
Options Q8: two sets of numbers a chapter with 10 people each, as written, which makes 9 sets in the take, one over rule 18's "about 8" (marked)? Or one set with 16 to 20 people a chapter?
Rulebook Q7: may Nani ever call you "beta"? Written here: no family word for you at all.
Options Q14: should your reply after a pick name only the job ("Berths, sorted"), as written, or the person? Names would show your picks when you scroll back up.
Rulebook Q6: what does a Hinglish bubble look like, "Today you're in charge" or "Aaj tum in-charge ho"?
Rulebook Q14: should spoken lines count towards the word caps? The bible is written to the proposed caps anyway (10 words a line, 120 a chapter, 80 for the opening).
Options Q10: the title Saal Bhar, once the Play Store, App Store, Indian trademark and regional film checks are done.

New: the take has about 60 names (5 household, 5 chapter voices, 50 card people), close to the old take's 62. Circles of eight would cut ten names but cannot meet rule 17, because the weakest card in an early decision would later have to sit in a pair.

New: the cousins (chapter 1) and the wedding relatives (chapter 5) carry names that mark no community, as one family's would, while the neighbours, applicants and lane players are mixed (Muslim, Christian, Bengali and Gujarati pairs). Is that the balance you want? Nagsen, Kusum and Lalit sit on cards but never in a pair.

New: eight new faces to paint, one portrait each in one look (Asha, Sapna, Kavita, Vinod and Pankaj in Station; Manju in Cricket; Rekha and Satish in Jadugar), through the heavy queue, with the close-up check.

New, for the readers rather than for you: chapter 3 (the family shop) and chapter 5 (a lane wedding with lent rooms) are the most likely to fail the six-player test, for the Bengaluru analyst and the retired officer in Coimbatore.

verdicts.beat: 1.19, 1.20, 1.21 (D3) against 1.31, 1.32 (D7), the hard twin. Merges the measure flag on 1.20/1.32 with the rules flag on 1.19 to 1.21.
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 23: 'Every decision says whether being picked is a gain (the seat, the trip) or a load (the 2 am shift): a load is asked as a split or marked as a chore in the game, and unless all five players asked agree which it is, it stays out of the twins.' Rule 20: 'A reason that truly matters (holds a driving licence, saw it happen) sits only on the equal two of a 'matters' twin, one a chapter in the First take, never on a decoy.'
verdicts.breaks: D3's 'gain' means going alone through a door that slides shut (1.21) into a dim, empty coach (1.19 and the D3 backdrop). That turns Kiran's 'A stranger kept following her last trip' into a reason that really bears on the task: is it safe to send her? Rule 20 allows such a reason only on the chapter's one 'matters' twin. At D7 the same fact has nothing to do with a bench. So a player who protects whoever was followed keeps Kiran back (picks Uday), then gives Chetan the bench. That is the man both times, read as a lean towards men from a choice that ignored gender. D3 is also a twin decision with a doubtful gain and no mark for the five players, so under rule 23 it should not be in a twin yet. Two parts are not shown. 'Quiet coach' claims no Indian Railways designation, since Papa only says the next coach is quieter, and rule 1 is a test for readers, not for the writer. And the panels paint the train, which is the setting, as rule 26 allows.
verdicts.fix: Keep D3 inside the family's lit bay, with a gain that has nothing to do with going off alone, for example 'One spare pillow. Who gets it?'. Then the report bears on neither half's task. Do not use another lower berth (the measure checker's example): it repeats D1's role in the same place, which rule 6 forbids. Drop 'quiet coach' from 1.19, the question and the confirm button. Repaint 1.19, 1.21 and the D3 backdrop as the lit bay with no shutting door, and keep 1.31 matching it (rule 37). Mark D3 and D7 [WAITS rule 23: the five players agree it is a gain].

verdicts.rule_text: 'The equal two really compete for the same place: a player who goes only by the first number, or only by the second, still has to choose between them, and the build refuses any plain or hard decision that fails.'
verdicts.breaks: The numbers confirm it. At D3 Vivek has 5 hours slept, the pair's own figure, so a player going by sleep alone can give the seat to Vivek. At D4 Kiran has 1 missed train, like the pair, so a player led by target 2 fills the second pouch from a three-way tie. At D7 Hetal ties the pair on hours on feet (9) and Vivek ties them on hours slept (5). D3 and D7 are hard and D4 is plain, so rule 14 says the build refuses all three. The options file (Part C, step 4) also makes this check a condition before the owner sees the sample. The writer's check only looked for cards tied on both numbers. Severity raised from weakens, because the rule itself stops the build.
verdicts.fix: For D3 and D7, take the tested variant in /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-priyanshu-Sex-Ed/f50ea7ee-0855-46a2-8572-0aa08df5b855/scratchpad/blend/check-1/variant-d3-d7.json: set A becomes 15/4 for Kiran and Uday and 10/4 for Nirmala and Chetan, which also makes Chetan 10/4 at D1. For D4, re-run the solver with 'no third card on the pair's value on either number'. Then re-check the weakest-card reading for Kiran before D8.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 22: 'Gossip about card people appears only as such notes, on at least two cards besides the equal two, and each chapter's judging notes come from at least two people, women and men.' The rulebook defines the equal two as 'the hidden woman and man on a decision's cards'.
verdicts.breaks: Not for the reasons given. No rule asks a screen to judge women and men equally, or to show the same voices in both halves. Rule 37 binds the asker's bubbles, not the card notes, and the chapter does have two voices, Papa and Mausi. But rule 22 does break. Read per decision (the equal two belong to one decision), 'at least two cards besides the equal two' fails in the second half of both judging twins. Besides the pair, only Vivek carries gossip at D5 and only Neha at D8, against two cards at D1 and two at D4. So in the first halves the loaded note hides among two other judging notes, and in the second halves among one. That is the imbalance the checker sensed. The three-way tie on trains missed at D4 belongs to the rule 14 entry.
verdicts.fix: Re-run the deck solver with rule 22 read per decision: at least two judging notes besides the pair at D1, D4, D5 and D8, and each voice's notes split between women and men. At D5 the only free card is Neha, who is in the D6 pair, so rule 17 then also needs a judging note on Uday before D6 (at D4). If no deck can keep rules 17 and 22 together, put that clash to the owner.

verdicts.beat: 1.20 (D3) and 1.32 (D7) notes, with the 1.07 title card and the 1.17 key. Merges the measure and rules flags on the hard pair's wording.
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 28: 'A hard fact means the same for a woman and a man: 'bullying', not 'harassment', at work, and 'refused to give dowry' against 'took no dowry' fails; every hard pair is read by the five Hindi-first players before it ships.' Rule 36: 'Before and during a decision, no bubble, caption or sign names, points at, describes, or uses the note words of anyone on that decision's cards'.
verdicts.breaks: The two halves do not state the same fact at the same weight. Kiran's 'A stranger kept following her last trip' | 'पिछले सफ़र में अजनबी पीछा करता रहा' is recent and names a stranger. Chetan's 'Someone kept trailing him along a platform once' | 'एक बार प्लेटफ़ॉर्म पर कोई उसके पीछे लगा रहा' is vague and could be any time, and पीछे लगा रहना is softer than पीछा करना. Only Kiran's note repeats the title card's word ('followed' | पीछा at 1.07). The title card is a sign shown before D3, so rule 36 bars this, and it makes her case read as the chapter's topic. Her 'trip' | सफ़र also repeats the 'Night trips' | 'रात के सफ़र' key shown at D2. In English, 'following her last trip' can also read as 'following her previous trip'. The writer sent the pair to the readers but did not mark the break.
verdicts.fix: Write both notes to one time frame and one strength, in new words in each half (rule 16). Use 'last journey' | यात्रा, not 'trip' | सफ़र, and no word from the title card in either note (or reword the title card instead). For example, Kiran: 'A stranger tailed her on her last journey.'; Chetan: 'On his last journey, a stranger shadowed him.' (8 and 8 words). Rebalance each screen's note lengths, and let the five Hindi-first readers choose Hindi verbs of equal strength.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 21: 'Inside a pair both names mark the same community or neither does, and community-marked names sit in pairs, on decoys, at the top and at the bottom as often as their share.'
verdicts.breaks: Confirmed. The only community-marked names hold 3 of the chapter's 5 clearest bottom places against a share of 2 in 10, and they lead only inside their own pair at D5. The writer flagged it in the notes, but none of these five beats carries the mark the owner asked for. The rule 17 sub-point (Mehul looked weakest at D2 and then sits in the D5 pair) depends on what 'weakest' means, which rule 17 does not define. On the writer's 'beaten on both numbers' reading it passes; on the average-place reading it fails.
verdicts.fix: Put [BREAKS rule 21] on 1.17, 1.26, 1.29, 1.32 and 1.35, and take one of the writer's exits: names that mark no community for the cousins, accept the break, or loosen rule 17. Ask the owner to define 'weakest' when they tick rule 17.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 25: 'the chapter opens and closes warm without joking about it'. Rule 40: 'Every beat reads without its picture and at double text size, with bubbles stacked under it'.
verdicts.breaks: The last story beat, a wet back step with a tumbler on its side, is a worry, so the chapter does not close warm. The writer called it a 'risk', not a break. Its fact is also told only by the picture. With no picture, at 200% text or on a screen reader, the beat says only 'That evening. Nani's back step.', which breaks rule 40 and the spec's rule that 'a picture that alone carries a fact gets that fact in words'. The words cannot go in the narration box, which rule 35 keeps for time and place. The five-beat ending is already marked [BREAKS rule 42] at 1.41. Moving 1.40 to open chapter 2, as the flag suggests, only moves the break, because rule 25 also asks a chapter to open warm.
verdicts.fix: End chapter 1 on 1.39 and 1.41. In chapter 2's first scene, after a warm opening beat, tell the slip in words as a household line rather than by a picture alone. Chapter 1's ending then runs 1.37, 1.38, 1.39 and 1.41, still marked [BREAKS rule 42].

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 9: 'The household: 4 to 8 people met on one screen in the opening, each with a plain relation label'. Rule 10: 'The household are the voices who ask, gossip and joke'. Rule 33: 'The household is painted only in the present-day style ... In a world's panels they are seen from behind or speak from off the panel, always with a name tag.'
verdicts.breaks: Mausi is family and she gossips (her face chip sits on six judging notes), so under rule 10 she is household. But she is not on the opening's household screen (1.03, rule 9), and she is painted face-on in Lugdi (rule 33). The rulebook has two casts, the household and the circle; the bible's 'chapter voices' are a third cast it does not have. This holds whatever the answer to Q11: if no, she breaks rules 9 and 33; if yes, she is removed. One part is not shown: a quirk. One shout a chapter is an allowed bubble kind (rule 35), and nothing on the beat makes her the comic one.
verdicts.fix: Mark 1.09 [BREAKS rules 9 and 33: a one-chapter family voice outside the household] [WAITS rulebook Q11]. Until Q11 is answered, either add Mausi to the household screen and paint her from behind or off the panel, or accept the marked break.

verdicts.rule_text: 'Both halves sit four decisions apart, with one lead-in per scene rather than per decision'.
verdicts.breaks: The writer's own four scenes open at 1.13, 1.19, 1.25 and 1.31, yet each second decision also gets its own lead-in. That makes eight lead-ins, four beats and four paintings more than the rule allows, and brings back the 'lead-in, cards' rhythm the clarity judge marked down. One part is not shown: 'it happened' beats without a change of place. Rule 39 allows them when they are the same for every pick; only the bible limits them to a change of place.
verdicts.fix: Drop 1.16, 1.22, 1.28 and 1.34. Put each second decision's need either on the 'it happened' beat before it, as a fixed off-panel line that is the same for every pick, or in the question (D4's 'Who holds the two cash pouches?' already does this). Keep Papa's dead phone somewhere before D2 (see the entry on 1.16 and 1.28).

verdicts.rule_text: 'Decision screens keep their limits, a question of at most 10 words and 15 counted words on the screen, with card notes held by the note-length rule instead'.
verdicts.breaks: The house counter (design-system/tools/frames.cjs) counts every visible word except names, quotes and screen-reader text. So the top bar counts too: 'Back', 'Chapter' and 'of', the clock's 'pm, Coach S4' and the '?'. At D1 the question has 5 words, the key 5, the button 2 and the cut plate 1, and the top bar adds about 7, so the screen comes to 16 to 20 depending on what is showing. The writer's '10 to 15' left the top bar out. The words rule 50 adds (the story clock and 'Chapter 1 of 5') are what push it over. The owner has complained about too much text three times.
verdicts.fix: Make Back an icon, show progress as the calendar ring with '1/5' in figures, give the clock the time only ('9:45 pm'), and keep confirm labels short ('Send to the quiet coach' goes with the D3 fix). Then measure every stop with frames.cjs before calling it passed.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 23: 'Every decision says whether being picked is a gain (the seat, the trip) or a load (the 2 am shift) ... and unless all five players asked agree which it is, it stays out of the twins.' Rule 65: 'the Hindi is written fresh in everyday spoken words and read aloud by five Hindi-first players'.
verdicts.breaks: The bench is offered as 'a warm seat', but this is a May dawn, when most of India is at its hottest, and the Hindi 'वेटिंग रूम गरम है' says the room is hot. Many players will read the bench as somewhere to avoid, so the hard twin's second half may turn from a gain into a load, and D7 carries no [WAITS rule 23] mark. Rules 1 and 65 on their own are tests for readers, and the text alone does not show them broken.
verdicts.fix: 'Waiting room has a fan. One bench free.' | 'वेटिंग रूम में पंखा है। एक बेंच ख़ाली।', with the gain 'a seat under the fan', kept within 2 words of the new 1.19. Mark D7 [WAITS rule 23].

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 15: 'The equal two are never the only tie: from chapter 2 on, at least half the decisions also show two women or two men tied'. Options A4: 'Second ties (rule 9 below) come in everyday decisions too, chapter 1 included.'
verdicts.breaks: It is true that the pair is the only full tie in 8 of 8 decisions. But rule 15 as written starts at chapter 2, so this chapter does not break it. The options file says the opposite for this very sample: the A4 list, which Part C step 4 makes a pass condition, includes chapter 1, while A5 rule 9 says the rule counts only after the research check. This depends on a call the owner has not been asked, and it is not among the rulebook's 16 questions: is chapter 1 exempt (rule 15 as written) or included (A4 and A5 rule 9)? If included, 0 of 8 is far short of half.
verdicts.fix: Ask the owner in one plain line whether chapter 1 also needs ties between two women or two men. If yes, re-run the solver with such a tie in at least four decisions, loosening rule 17 where it cannot fit. If no, add a note to rule 15 that chapter 1 is exempt on purpose.

verdicts.rule: 15 (flagged as 14 and 15), and the options file's A4 list
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 15: 'in rank, team, batting order and split the equal two are the top two in at most half the decisions.' Options A4: 'The shapes repeated: the equal two always level at the top, or one card above and one below. In rank, team and split decisions their place varies (sometimes below the cut or tied for last).'
verdicts.breaks: The shape is as described: in all four decisions, on each number, one card sits above the pair and one below. The rulebook does not forbid this. Rule 15 only caps how often the pair are the top two (here 0 of 4), and rule 14 is met. It is the repeated shape the A4 list names, and Part C step 4 proposes holding the sample to that list. That depends on the owner approving Part C step 4, which has not happened. Note that in a team decision the pair cannot sit below the cut without breaking rule 14, because a player going by one number would never reach them. So only rank and split decisions can vary the shape.
verdicts.fix: In twin A's two ranks, put the pair tied for third, or tied first, the same way in both halves. A rank still makes a player who goes by one number put the two in order. Leave D4 and D8 at the cut for rule 14, and re-run the solver with the variation as a constraint.

verdicts.rule: 11 (and options A4, 'Jobs that carry a gender script')
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 11: 'The circle goes against type at least as often as with it, judged from an agreed list of typed jobs.' Options A4: 'Jobs that carry a gender script: berths, pills, the bank card, jewellery keys, wet sacks, bowling. These are checked before panels are written, and people go against type at least as often as with it.'
verdicts.breaks: On the writer's own count, the circle's jobs go against type 4 to 3, so rule 11 passes as far as it can be checked. But the rule rests on an agreed list that does not exist yet, and A4 leaves 'jobs that carry a gender script' as an open item to check before panels are written. The chapter records no such check for the lower berths (on A4's list), the cash pouches (close to its 'bank card'), riding first, or the free seat. The pattern in the plain notes is real: food and water go to women (Hetal's water can and sandwiches, Nirmala's tiffins, Kiran's dal) and kit goes to men (Mehul's blankets, lock and umbrellas, Uday's first-aid box and carrom board). If those scripts hold, twins A and D can read a player who follows family scripts as one who follows the nudge. This depends on the owner agreeing the typed list (rule 11), on closing A4's open item, and on whether helpful acts count as jobs.
verdicts.fix: Before panels are written, put the roles (lower berth, hot plate, holding the cash, riding first, the free seat) to the five players together with rule 23's gain question. Swap some helpful acts across genders (for example, Mehul made the sandwiches and Hetal has the spare lock and chain), keeping rule 19's note lengths.

verdicts.rule_text: 'The equal two really compete for the same place: a player who goes only by the first number, or only by the second, still has to choose between them, and the build refuses any plain or hard decision that fails.'
verdicts.breaks: Hetal ties the pair on trains missed (2) at D2, and Mehul ties them on night trips (2) at D6, so the first sentence of rule 14 is broken. The build refusal covers only plain and hard decisions, and in this 'matters' twin the charged phone decides anyway, so polish is the right severity.
verdicts.fix: Fold it into the D4 solver re-run if it comes free; otherwise leave it.

verdicts.beat: Note words echoed earlier: lines at 1.05, 1.07, 1.11, 1.12, the 1.17 key, 1.19 and 1.21 against notes at 1.17, 1.20, 1.23, 1.26, 1.29 and 1.35; props at 1.09, 1.10, 1.14, 1.15 and 1.23. Merges the two rule 36 echo flags.
verdicts.rule_text: 'Before and during a decision, no bubble, caption or sign names, points at, describes, or uses the note words of anyone on that decision's cards ('Pune', 'the baby'); decoys stay as card notes, not bubbles.'
verdicts.breaks: These words break the rule. 'Coach' | डिब्बा in the 1.12 narration and the clocks comes before Hetal's 'in the coach' | 'डिब्बे में' at D6. 'Seat' | सीट at 1.19 and 1.21 comes before Vivek's 'window seat' at D5. D8's own key says 'Trains missed' next to Kiran's 'Trains new staff' (English only). The D2 key's 'trip' | सफ़र comes before Kiran's D3 note. The measure script also found two that neither flag lists: फ़ोन at 1.05 before Vivek's D2 note, and खाना at 1.11 before Chetan's D4 note. The writer's claim that no note word appears earlier is false, because the check looked back only to the previous decision. These parts are not shown: 'Coaches' and 'coaching' are different words, and rule 36 covers bubbles, captions and signs, not paintings, so the painted blankets, chain-lock and tiffin carrier break nothing. Mausi carrying tiffins at 1.09 against Nirmala's tiffin note is a small continuity point.
verdicts.fix: Check every line from 1.01 onwards against every later note, in both languages, and reword either the note or the earlier line: 'Shows new staff the ropes at a bank.', 'last journey' (see the hard-pair entry), 'Hogs the window, always.', 'for everyone here' instead of 'in the coach', and a new word for 1.05's फ़ोन and 1.11's खाना or for the notes that repeat them. Optionally have Mausi carry only bags at 1.09.

verdicts.rule_text: 'Inside a pair, the two match on how they appeared earlier that chapter: on the same number of cards, as high on the numbers each time (both in the top half of those cards, or both in the bottom half), with notes of the same warmth'.
verdicts.breaks: 'Each time' asks for matching appearance by appearance. Uday was clearly top at D3 (first on both numbers), while Neha was never in the top half: tied 2nd and 3rd at D1, and top on one number but bottom on the other at D5. Kiran was clearly top at D3, while Prakash's best was the middle tie at D1. The pairs match only on the writer's 'same mix' reading, which the rule's wording does not give.
verdicts.fix: Re-run the solver with place-by-place matching, or reword rule 17 to the mix reading when the owner ticks it.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 11: 'Each chapter's circle is 8 to 10 new people, half women and half men, all the same kind of relation to the household ..., with no quirks'.
verdicts.breaks: 'Brought the carrom board, as always' is a habit, a warm quirk in a plain note, and rule 11 gives the circle no quirks (rule 9 keeps them for the household). Judging notes are different: they are gossip from a named voice, which rule 22 allows. Rule 16 says nothing about the un-nudged member's note.
verdicts.fix: Give Uday a plain 6-word fact at D6, for example 'Repairs bicycles at the weekly market.'

Rule 13: every decision has 4 or 5 cards, exactly one woman and one man tied on both numbers, no second woman-and-man tie, and ages within 8 (the widest gap is 7, Pooja and Chetan at D4).

Rule 14 holds wherever no third card ties the equal two: D1, D5 and D8 on both numbers, D2, D3 and D4 on the first number, D6 on the second. No card beats the equal two on either number in a pick one, and exactly one card sits above them on each number in every rank and team.
Rule 15's cap: the equal two are never the top two in a rank or team (0 of 4).

Rule 16: in all four twins, both halves are the same kind with the same asker, share no one in the equal two, and put the nudge on the other gender. The nudge notes share at most two words (no one-word swap, no her-to-his swap), and the nudge's voice stays the same across halves (Mausi in twin A, Papa in twin D).

Rule 17: no pair repeats; nobody is in more than two pairs or in pairs two decisions running; no pair's numbers return under the same number names; who is older changes sides in every twin (level at D5); and no card that every other card beat or equalled on both numbers sits in a later pair (the only one is Mehul at D8, the last decision).
Rule 18: every card keeps its numbers wherever its set shows, all numbers are within 0 to 20, and the chapter uses two sets.

Rule 19: notes are within 2 words of each other in every decision, in English and Hindi; the equal two's notes are the same length in both languages in all 8; their notes never open on the same word; and the longest note falls on the two in 3 of 8 counting ties (2 of 8 alone), inside rule 19's quarter to a half.

Rule 20: every decision has a decoy whose note is of the nudge's kind; both hard decisions put a heavy fact on a decoy (Prakash at D3, Vivek at D7); no heavy fact sits on a community-marked name; the only reasons that truly matter are the charged phones on the matters twin's equal two.

Rule 21: inside every pair, both names mark the same community or neither does (Hetal and Mehul, both Gujarati, at D5). No card note carries a relation word in English or Hindi, and the circle page shows names only.

Rule 22: judging notes come from a woman (Mausi) and a man (Papa) and sit on six cards besides the equal two; none says anything about women or men in general, and nobody doubts the report of being followed.

Rule 36: no card person's name appears in any bubble, sign or narration, and no bubble points at a single card person. Papa's battery lines point at the charged-phone reason, which sits on the equal two in both halves of the matters twin, as designed.

Rule 37: Papa asks all eight decisions, in his bubble on plain and matters decisions and in the plain box on D3 and D7. Both halves of each twin have the same number of lead-in bubbles, with the asker's words within 1, questions within 2 words in both languages, and the same single figure seen from behind.

Rules 43 to 45: every bar sits at or below the equal two's numbers. All 14,400 answer sets for the four target decisions were tried: all three stamps can happen, swapping the equal two never changes a count or the stamp, and always the woman and always the man both end with both targets met. A player who goes by the first number only and one who goes by the second only both land on the middle stamp. The cards that can miss a bar are 2 women and 2 men, and the matters and hard decisions feed nothing.
Rule 63: every question is 10 words or fewer in English and Hindi.
Rules 39 and 25: every settled plate and 'it happened' panel is the same for every pick and names nobody; Papa's closing line changes by stamp only; the stamp never lands on a hard decision.

Owner answers 2 to 5: the player is the grown-up child of the house (calls them Mummy and Papa, older than Tinku at 21, 'Everyone calls you anyway'), never painted and given no gender word. The chapter reads as one strip with eight stops and settled plates that name nobody. Lugdi is only the look, and its big moment, the cover reprint, falls on the outcome at 1.37. The writer marked rule 42 at 1.41, rules 21 and 18, and the waits on rulebook Q9, Q14, Q16, Q6 and options Q14.

Rule 7: no hand, sleeve, body or shadow of the player in any painting. The only hand-over is Mummy's pen at 1.05, in the present-day opening, painted the instant before. Inside Lugdi nothing is held out; the list lies on the berth (1.10).
Rule 8 and the bubble spec's rule 10: nobody says bhaiya, didi or beta. The player is only 'you' or 'in charge' (इंचार्ज).

Rule 66: every Hindi line to or from the player marks no gender. Commands (क्रम लगाओ), 'who should' asks in the subjunctive (रखे? जाए? करे? मिले?), lines where the player is not the doer (आज रात इंचार्ज तुम हो, सब तुम्हें ही फ़ोन करते हैं), polite forms to elders (पेन दीजिए, लिस्ट दिखाइए, चलिए), and the game's own voice in आप forms (चुनें, दें, भेजें, शुरू करें). There is no -ेगा, -ोगे or -ूँगा future anywhere.

Rule 62, counted the proposed way: the opening has 42 EN / 48 HI (cap 80). The story beats come to 105 / 110 as the writer counts them. No beat goes over 20 words, the longest spoken line is 7 words, no narration goes over 12, and every beat but 1.07 has at most 3 pieces. Under your standing rule, which leaves speech out, the chapter including the title card is 69 / 75.
Rule 63: every question is 10 words or fewer (the longest is 7), and every outcome beat is 20 or fewer (1.38 has 18 / 19).
Rule 64: no 'test', 'bias', 'attitude' or 'twin' on screen, and no please, sorry, oops or well done in the game's voice or the outcome.
Rule 35: all eight narration boxes give only time and place, there is one shout in the chapter, and no thought bubbles.

Rule 36: no card name in any bubble, caption or sign before or during a decision, except the circle page that rule 11 asks for. No gossip in bubbles, and decoys stay on the cards (apart from the battery lines flagged above).

Rule 37: Papa asks all eight decisions, never sits on a card and is never the comic one. D3 and D7 put the question in the plain box. Twins B and D match in bubbles and words. Across the take the askers are 3 women and 2 men.

Rules 38 and 39: three fixed 'You' lines ('Okay. The pen.', 'Show me the list.', 'Let's go in.') that never name or judge anyone. Every 'it happened' beat and settled plate is the same for every pick.

Rules 31 to 33: card people are never painted, every decision backdrop is free of people, Papa is seen from behind or heard off the panel in every Lugdi panel, household face chips are present-day, at most two painted people in any panel, and the first speaker is on the left at 1.04.
Rule 30: the phone, list, platform name board, number plates and clock face are painted blank or plain, and months, dates, rings and stamps are all live text.

Rules 2, 3 and 48: no year on screen, present-day props, no festival, ritual, religious symbol or brand. The shop calendar's picture is a mountain, not a deity, and an 80th birthday is an allowed event. Rule 4: no money amounts and no domestic help.

Rules 11 and 12: ten cousins from Mummy's side, 5 women and 5 men aged 27 to 37, met by name only on the circle page with no quirks. Against type at least as often as with it, and that still holds if Uday's embroidery counts as with type. No persona names (Shruti, Ravi, Sunita, Meena, Natarajan, Farida, Lakshmi) are reused.

Rules 25 to 27 and 29: one hard topic that the train journey really holds (M21), arriving as cousins' own past cases, never the household's. It never reaches a story panel or bubble, the title card names it before Start, the help line sits only in '?', and Lugdi's big moment never lands on a hard decision.

Rules 42 to 46: the outcome comes only after the last pick. Every bar sits at or below the equal two (9 under 11, 9 at 9, 1 at 1, 1 at 1), and all three stamps can happen. The cards that miss a bar are 2 women and 2 men. The 'matters' twin has a fixed outcome. Papa's band lines are warm, about the event, and name nobody, and the stamped list carries only the job and the count.

Rules 47 to 51: one present-day frame, an opening with at most two painted people a panel, and chapter 1 the most familiar event. 8 decisions and 4 twins, each pair four apart. The story clock is on every decision. Progress is the calendar ring, filling by eighths and told apart by shape as well as colour. Three kinds (Rank, Pick one, Pick a team), each shown by a moving hand the first time.
British spelling throughout (grey, fertiliser, centre), and no em or en dashes.

Six-player test, predicted, for real readers to confirm. Ravi (26, Indore, lives with his parents and a younger sister) is the closest match and passes. Shruti (27, Bengaluru, from Mysuru) passes on the event, and the English labels carry the northern kin words. Meena (30, Gumla) passes, since the overnight family train is common there, apart from the city-only lift mechanic. Farida (32, takes the train every day) passes, apart from the Mausi kin word. Sunita (41, Sitapur) passes on the event and plays a younger grandchild, by your own 25 Oct choice. Mr Natarajan (61, Coimbatore) passes on the event, plays a grandchild by the same choice, and a South Indian reader still has to check the kin labels. Weak spots for all six are the 'quiet coach' (D3) and the 'warm' waiting room in May (D7).

verdicts.rule_text: 'The equal two are never the only tie: from chapter 2 on, at least half the decisions also show two women or two men tied, and in rank, team, batting order and split the equal two are the top two in at most half the decisions.'
verdicts.breaks: Checked against chapter-2.json. No decision shows a second tie: 0 of 8, against a floor of 4. In all four pick ones the two are the single best card on both numbers (D2 7/14, D3 9/22, D6 5/18, D7 3/10), so the only tie on screen is always the top woman and man. The writer marked this. The writer's own solver found no line-up that works while each person keeps fixed numbers, so the cause is the bible's number scheme, not a slip in the writing. The split cap holds: in D1 and D5 the two are not the top two.
verdicts.fix: Give each scene its own slip, so a person's numbers are no longer fixed. This also ends the stale-morning and pair-number problems below. Then in each pick one put a same-sex decoy tie below the two (for example, both of D2's decoys men at 2 and 7). Add another same-sex tie in at least two of the Splits and checks. The writer's other way out, a Rank in set B, also answers the back-to-back pick ones.

verdicts.beat: 2.01 (whole chapter: one hard twin, B at 2.10 and 2.22)
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 25: '...and the home chapter carries two, never as the frame of a chapter or a day.' Rule 50: 'except the home chapter: one "matters", two hard, one plain, unless you change it (question 3).' Question 3: 'Until you say, it stays two.'
verdicts.breaks: Chapter 2 is the home chapter (Rukavat, 'Home and family', rule 49). It carries one hard twin and two plain ones. Your 22 Oct call of two hard twins stands until you answer question 3, so the chapter as written breaks a decision of yours that is still in force. The writer marked this correctly ([BREAKS rules 25 and 50] [WAITS rulebook Q3]). The chapter cannot go ahead as written while the call stands.
verdicts.fix: Answer question 3. If you choose two, twin D turns hard using the bible's care facts, read by the five Hindi-first players (rule 28). Note that hard decisions in this chapter feed no target. Turning D4 and D8 hard would leave target 2 (cots and taxi seats) with no decisions, so the target list and 2.31 would need rewriting. If you choose one, nothing changes here.

verdicts.beat: 2.06, 2.07 (D1, the night chair at Nani's bedside)
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 12: 'Everyone on a card, speaking or choosing is 18 or over, in a role a woman or a man could hold in India today that means the same for both...' Rule 20: 'A reason that truly matters ... sits only on the equal two of a "matters" twin...'
verdicts.breaks: The load is sitting all night at an 80-year-old woman's bedside in a ward. In many Indian homes that is a woman's job (help to the toilet, changing her), and many wards expect a woman patient's night attendant to be a woman. Either way, the role does not mean the same for Deepa and Rajan. In a Split, fewer chores counts as the favour (reading.ts favoured()), so a player who follows the custom loads Deepa and reads as favouring the man. The flag calls twin A lopsided, but that is not quite right: D5's 'Clothes' job pulls the same way (see that entry). So both halves lean the same side, which is worse for the reading. A nurse reader should confirm the ward practice, but the home custom alone is enough to break rule 12.
verdicts.fix: Move the turns away from the bedside: make them night turns on the corridor bench by the ward door, holding the attendant pass and the family phone, where women and men wait alike. Ask a nurse reader, and the six-player readers (rule 1), before rewriting. Change D5's 'Clothes' as well.

verdicts.beat: 2.07 and 2.19 (Split, twin A), 2.16 and 2.28 (Spend checks, twin D)
verdicts.rule_text: 'The equal two really compete for the same place: a player who goes only by the first number, or only by the second, still has to choose between them, and the build refuses any plain or hard decision that fails.'
verdicts.breaks: Confirmed in the code. Pick.tsx lets the checks step go live with one card chosen, Split.tsx lets one person take every chore, and favoured() in reading.ts returns null when the two get the same. So one cot to Rajan (D4) or one seat to Nagsen (D8) meets target 2 without touching the two. Likewise, all three turns to Uma (D1) or all three jobs to Yasmin (D5) meet target 1. These are both plain twins, half of the chapter's measured decisions. The result is lost readings, not a false lean, so 'weakens' is right, although rule 14's build refusal still applies. The 2.31 line-2 flag under rule 42 has the same cause (see that entry).
verdicts.fix: Make these checks take exactly two, which rule 51's 'checks spending up to 2' allows. Make each Split one turn per person, and say so in the need line ('3 turns, 3 different people').

verdicts.rule_text: 'Nothing else that follows gender sits on the same side in both halves (age, who is older, who grew up in the house, who travels).'
verdicts.breaks: Confirmed from the numbers. In D4 the numbers put Rajan first (14 hours on his feet, slept 6), and in D8 Nagsen (16 and 1): a man both times. A player who gives the two places to one woman and one man therefore picks Uma, then Ganga, the woman in both halves, with no help from the notes. Rule 17's examples do not name this, but it is something that follows gender sitting on the same side in both halves. Twin A is one-sided rather than same-side. In D1 the two sure turns go to Uma and Mumtaz (slept 8 and 7), so a balancing player loads Rajan. In D5 the sure picks are Yasmin and Dinesh, one of each.
verdicts.fix: Make the first-placed card a woman in one half of twin D (for example, make D4's most tired card a woman). In D1, make the two sure picks one woman and one man, or make D5's two sure picks both men.

verdicts.beat: 2.07 against 2.16, 2.18, 2.19, 2.27, 2.28 (night turns, then cots, morning jobs and taxi seats)
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 17: 'Inside a pair, the two match on how they appeared earlier that chapter...' Rule 20: 'A reason that truly matters (holds a driving licence, saw it happen) sits only on the equal two of a "matters" twin...'
verdicts.breaks: The cited rules are not broken as written. Rule 43 asks only that decisions come before the outcome in story time, rule 1 is the six-player test and rule 5 is about what you are asked. The stale numbers ('on their feet 16 hours today' at 8:30 am) are a story fault with no rule behind them; the writer already flags them at 2.18 and in note 8. What does break the rules is the overlap. D1's Split lets you put Uma or Mumtaz in the night chair, and each is later half of a pair (Uma in D4, Mumtaz in D5) whose partner, Dinesh or Firoz, was never on D1's cards. If Mumtaz sat 4 to 7, she is in the chair at 6:00 and her 'slept 7' cannot be true. Sparing her a job is then a real reason, and the reading counts it as favouring her. So a reason that matters sits on a plain twin's pair, created by your own earlier pick, and the two no longer match on how they appeared earlier.
verdicts.fix: Keep all five of D1's cards out of the set-A pairs that follow (D4, D5), and preferably off the 11:30 pm and 6:00 am cards. Either relabel set A in this chapter 'On feet by 9 pm' | 'Slept the night before', or give the morning a fresh slip that fits the clock. Never let the numbers follow your picks, which would make the two unequal. Re-run the line-up search after the change.

verdicts.beat: 2.10, 2.22 (twin B, the hard twin: the house quarrel on the key and the purse)
verdicts.rule: 25 (and 20); merges the measure flag on rules 20 and 26 with the rules flag on rule 25
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 25: 'Every chapter carries one hard topic that its own event really holds (dowry talk in a wedding week, being followed home after a late shift)...' Rule 20: 'A reason that truly matters ... sits only on the equal two of a "matters" twin...'
verdicts.breaks: The everyday-moments file names the care burden as the hard topic of a parent's night in hospital (M06). A quarrel over a house belongs to M09, dividing the family house. A neighbour's quarrel with a sibling is not something the ward night holds, so rule 25 is broken. On rule 20: placed on Nani's house key (D2) and her purse (D6), the quarrel can read as a reason not to trust someone. But both halves are property or money tasks, so the measure flag's claim that 'D6 is less tied to property' is wrong. The effect is a hard twin that measures less, not a false lean. D6's lost-job decoy is the heavy decoy fact rule 20 asks for. No rule bars it, though beside a purse it invites a suspicion about money.
verdicts.fix: Make the care burden the hard topic, still a neighbour's own case (rule 27), on tasks with no property or money in them: the bedside locker key at D2, and at D6, for example, who sits with Nani while she waits for the X-ray. If question 3 gives two hard topics, the second must also be one the ward holds (M06 also lists who gives up work, and the cost). Keeping the quarrel means changing rule 25. Give D6's heavy decoy a fact with no money in it.

verdicts.rule: 28 (and 16); merges the measure and rules flags
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 28: 'A hard fact means the same for a woman and a man: "bullying", not "harassment", at work, and "refused to give dowry" against "took no dowry" fails; every hard pair is read by the five Hindi-first players before it ships.' Rule 16: '...never a near-copy (no one-word swap, no her-to-his swap).'
verdicts.breaks: Rule 28 is broken. 'Estranged from his brother' (a long break in contact) weighs more than 'Fell out with her sister'. पुश्तैनी मकान पर ... मनमुटाव (bad blood over the ancestral house) carries more of a property claim than पिता के मकान को लेकर ... अनबन. A daughter's quarrel over her father's house can still read as a daughter claiming a share, and giving each a same-sex sibling does not cure that. Rule 16 is not broken: the second note changes four parts (the verb, the pronoun, the sibling and whose home), which goes beyond the one-word and her-to-his swaps that rule 16 names.
verdicts.fix: Write both facts at one weight, in new words and different sentence shapes, within the decision's note length. Keep 'house', 'quarrel', घर and झगड़ा out (rule 36). Put the pair to the five Hindi-first players with one question: 'Does this mean the same for a woman and a man?' If they say no, move to the care fact (previous entry), which needs the same read.

verdicts.rule: 17 (warmth), with the rule 20 point as an aggravation
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 17: '...with notes of the same warmth...' Rule 20: '...A reason that truly matters ... sits only on the equal two of a "matters" twin, one a chapter in the First take, never on a decoy.'
verdicts.breaks: This is real, and the writer marked the warmth break. The flag adds a fair point. Uma's D2 decoy note, 'Has not been well since the winter fever', is a real reason to give her a cot two decisions later, and in D4 it points the same way as the nudge on Dinesh ('lazy'). D8 has the nudge alone. Rule 20 speaks of notes on the card in front of the player, so the carried reason makes the rule 17 break worse rather than counting as a second break.
verdicts.fix: Move D2's heavy fact to Nagsen, who is never in a pair. Use a fact no other chapter has (chapter 5 already has 'Lost his father to a fever in March') and give it a family word, which also mends the D2 decoy-kind entry. Give Uma a plain note in D2.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 23: 'Every decision says whether being picked is a gain (the seat, the trip) or a load (the 2 am shift): a load is asked as a split or marked as a chore in the game, and unless all five players asked agree which it is, it stays out of the twins.'
verdicts.breaks: 'Who rides home with Nani?' after her fall reads as an escort duty as much as a seat. Yet D8 carries no [WAITS rule 23] mark, while D2 and D6 do. D3 (going into the round) and D7 (explaining the medicines) could also read as duties. That gap is real. The other points break no rule as written. Every D8 card has been on their feet 12 hours or more (Uma exactly 12), so D8 can never change target 2. But rule 43 lets a decision feed a target, and the bar sits at or below the two as rule 45 requires. It does mean D8 adds nothing to rule 45's balance of misses. Seats 'booked for whenever the doctor lets Nani go' also leave the most tired waiting up to 12:30, which is a story-logic problem.
verdicts.fix: Make D8 a plain gain that cannot read as a duty, for example the 2 seats in the first auto back to the lane now, to sleep. Put one card below 12 hours on their feet so a miss is possible. Mark [WAITS rule 23] on D3, D7 and D8.

verdicts.rule: 16 and the twin definition (with rule 65's read)
verdicts.rule_text: Words used: 'A twin: a later decision of the same kind with a different equal two and the nudge on the other person.' Rule 16: '...the nudge on the other one, a new place and task, never a near-copy...' Rule 65: '...the Hindi is written fresh in everyday spoken words and read aloud by five Hindi-first players...'
verdicts.breaks: A twin moves the same nudge to the other person, and a heavier nudge is not the same one. The writer's painting notes claim 'the same weight', but the words do not bear that out. 'Dodges work' (कामचोर, someone who shirks on purpose) is harsher than 'Lazy' (आलसी). 'Snappy with everyone' (सब पर चिढ़ती है) is broader than 'moody' (मूडी है). Both heavier words fall on the woman's half. A player who resists a mild nudge but follows a strong one passes over Ganga in D8 and reads as leaning towards men.
verdicts.fix: Match the weight in new words of the same length: for D8, for example, 'Takes it easy, says Mausa ji' | 'मौसा जी कहते हैं, आराम-पसंद है', and drop 'with everyone' | 'सब पर' from D5. Put both twins to the five Hindi-first players.

verdicts.beat: 2.07, 2.16, 2.19 (decoy notes) and 2.07 (the nudge); 2.28 and plain notes checked
verdicts.rule_text: 'No situation, nudge wording or set of numbers is ever used twice, and a record of every one used lets the build refuse a repeat; a role may come back in a new place with a new nudge.'
verdicts.breaks: Checked against the other chapter files. Three of chapter 2's decoys reuse other chapters' nudges. 'Too chatty' (बहुत बातूनी) repeats 3.12's nudge 'Chatty at work' (बहुत बातूनी है). 'Too bossy' (रौब जमाती है) repeats 3.07's nudge, with the same Hindi. 'Fusses over everything' (नखरे) repeats 1.14's nudge 'Fusses over every little thing'. Chapter 2's own nudge, 'moody' (मूडी), was 1.23's decoy, 'Moody until her morning tea'. Two corrections to the flag. 'A show-off' is a decoy in 4.07, not its nudge, so it falls outside rule 6's 'nudge wording'. The repeated plain notes (tomatoes, tiffin, uniforms, maths) are outside rule 6 too, although 2.10's 'Stitches the school uniforms' nearly copies 3.07's 'Stitches school uniforms in June'.
verdicts.fix: Keep one take-wide list of judging words and give chapter 2 words that no other chapter uses ('nosy' and 'stubborn' appear in no chapter file). Also change the near-copy plain notes, although rule 6 does not require it.

verdicts.beat: 2.05 and the decisions (Nagsen in 2.07, 2.10, 2.22, 2.25, 2.28; Yasmin in 2.16; Mumtaz in 2.25)
verdicts.rule: 21; merges the measure flag with the rules flag on Nagsen's tag
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 21: '...mixed across communities in ordinary roles, and tagged in one list the build reads. Inside a pair both names mark the same community or neither does, and community-marked names sit in pairs, on decoys, at the top and at the bottom as often as their share.'
verdicts.breaks: Confirmed. Community-marked names are the bottom card in 5 of 8 decisions (Nagsen in D1, D2 and D6; Yasmin in D4; Mumtaz in D7), against their 40% share of the circle, and hold 4 of the 16 pair seats. The writer marked this. It is worse than the writer's note says. knowledge/content/cast.md records Nagsen as 'Marathi, a name common in Ambedkarite Buddhist families, many of them Dalit', but the bible tags him only 'Marathi'. So a name that may mark caste is the only card never in a pair and the weakest card in three decisions, in a take where caste belongs only to later weeks (rule 56). One small correction to the flag: in D7, Nagsen is not at an extreme (Mumtaz is lower).
verdicts.fix: Correct the tag in the bible's name list. Then either give Nagsen a woman with a Marathi name to pair with, or put the never-paired, low-numbered card on a name that marks no community. With a slip for each scene, keep marked names from landing at the bottom. Have the result read by people from the community shown.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 17: 'Nothing else that follows gender sits on the same side in both halves (age, who is older, who grew up in the house, who travels).'
verdicts.breaks: The writer marked this. The man is older in both halves (Yasmin 32 with Firoz 40; Uma 34 with Rajan 40), so a player who prefers the elder picks the man both times. Matters twins feed reading card 3. The flag's fix has a problem. Yasmin's library portrait is painted at 'about 32' (cast.md). Making her 44 on paper would break rule 13's 'portraits within 8 years of age' beside Firoz, and rule 33's library faces, unless she were repainted.
verdicts.fix: Use the bible's original D3 pair, Mumtaz (about 45) with Firoz (40), so the woman is older in one half. Then re-run the line-up search for the other rule 17 checks.

verdicts.beat: 2.03, 2.04, 2.09, 2.10 (where the family is; D2's spare key)
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 5: 'Ask the player only what someone in their place would really be asked...'
verdicts.breaks: This is real for D2. Chapter 1 ends with fourteen of the family at Nani's door, and the bible puts the cousins 'at the house with the little ones' that night. Nani's house is full, so nobody in your place would be asked which neighbour keeps its spare key tonight. The rest breaks no rule but players will notice it (Farida, who works on a ward, most of all): no beat says where Mummy, Nani's daughter, is, or why you, holding the one attendant pass, take no turn.
verdicts.fix: Make D2's object the bedside locker key that 2.09 already paints: 'My locker key. Someone keeps it tonight.' | 'मेरे लॉकर की चाबी। आज रात कोई रखे।' Say where Mummy is once, in Mausa ji's 2.03 line, for example 'Your Mummy's with the guests. The lane's downstairs.' | 'तुम्हारी मम्मी मेहमानों के साथ हैं। गली नीचे है।'

verdicts.beat: 2.30 (Rukavat's interruption card as a wordless frame)
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 2: 'Each world keeps its own big moment whatever the answer to question 2, such as Rukavat's "sorry for the interruption" card.' Rule 30: 'Rukavat's lettered slide and Hindi on signs become live text too, saying what they say now.' Rule 64: 'The house bans on "well done", "oops", "please", "sorry" and jokey feedback cover the game's own voice and every line in a chapter outcome...'
verdicts.breaks: Placing the card in the outcome forces the clash: rule 30 wants its words shown as live text, and rule 64 bans 'sorry' there. The writer chose rule 64 and left the frame wordless. That breaks rule 30 and may not read as the card at all, on the card your 21 Oct call named the world after. The writer cited rule 64 but did not mark the clash for you.
verdicts.fix: Mark [CLASH rules 2, 30 and 64] and ask you: keep the frame only, show the card's own line as live text with rule 64 relaxed for that one sign, or move the card to a mid-chapter beat with no hard topic (rule 25).

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 2: '...every painting prompt asks for present-day clothes and objects...' Rule 33: '...every new face passes the close-up check for painted bindis and lightened skin.'
verdicts.breaks: Chapter 2's look line asks for a present-day hospital and present-day objects, but never present-day clothes, so Mausa ji (2.03, 2.17) may be painted in 1980s dress, against your 'just the look' answer. I verified the pipeline problem. cutscenes.py paints Rukavat with wides.py's 'sunday' style ('Painted like a 1980s Indian family-magazine illustration... nostalgic Sunday light'). That style lacks the 'South Asian features and warm brown skin' that portraits.py added on 22 Oct because the same look painted pale faces. Rule 33 itself holds: writer note 21 promises the close-up check.
verdicts.fix: Add 'present-day clothes and objects' to chapter 2's look line. Add the skin-tone words to the 'sunday' story-panel style (a repo change, outside this read-only step). Do the close-up check on Mausa ji's face for lightened skin and painted dots.

verdicts.rule: 35 (and the story clock); merges the rules flags on the clock and on rule 35
verdicts.rule_text: Rule 35: '...a narration box for time and place only...' Rule 39: '...A short "it happened" beat after a pick (the auto pulls away) is fine when it is the same for every pick.'
verdicts.breaks: Two narration boxes tell events, which rule 35 keeps for time and place: '10:00. First turn.' (2.08) and '10:10. Round done.' (2.14). 2.08 also puts 10:00 between D1 at 9:15 and D2's lead-in at 9:20, so the clock reads 10:00, 9:20, 9:40, 10:10 and runs backwards. 'It happened' beats at an unchanged place (2.08, 2.11) break the bible's strip and the scroll design, not the rulebook. Rule 39 allows one after any pick, and the judges' graft asked for one after every commit. That part is a clash between the bible and the judges, not a rule break.
verdicts.fix: Drop 2.08. Make 2.14 just '10:10.' with its sound. 2.11 may stay under rule 39, or go if you keep the bible's change-of-place rule.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 43: '...every decision feeds one target or none and happens before the outcome in story time; the outcome stamps each target, and the number met falls in one of three bands set in advance (on time, a bit late, a rough night).'
verdicts.breaks: Rule 43's text is met: the targets come as a list at the start, each decision feeds one or none, 2.31 stamps each target, and the bands are set in advance. The rule does not say a band's label must follow from the targets. The judges' fix behind it does ('so a player can see why lunch was at 1:20'), and here the label does not follow. Who sat the chair or got a cot cannot change when the doctor sends Nani home. This depends on question 5 (whether the end may say how the event went at all). If you say yes, the label must be one the targets plausibly drive.
verdicts.fix: Stamp something the targets drive, for example 'Ready at the taxi: 9:00 / 9:30 / 10:15' | 'टैक्सी पर तैयार: ...' (rested people get the tea, chemist and bag done sooner), and change Nani's band lines to match.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 50: 'Both halves sit four decisions apart, with one lead-in per scene rather than per decision...' Rule 37: 'Both halves of a twin are asked by the same person, in the same number and shape of bubbles, words within 2, over a lead-in with the same figures and mood.'
verdicts.breaks: This is real, and it is not marked as a break or clash, although the writer explains it at 2.09 and 2.12. The flag overcounts. Six of the eight lead-ins open a new place or time (9:15 bed, 11:30 corridor, 6:00 ward, 7:30 X-ray, 8:00 window after X-ray, 8:30 taxi stand). Only 2.09 and 2.12 add lead-ins inside the ward scene, which the writer says holds D1 to D3. They exist because rule 37 wants each half of a twin over a matching lead-in, and the second halves of D2 and D3 (D6, D7) each open a new scene. So the rhythm complaint from the page-turn version does not apply here.
verdicts.fix: Mark [CLASH rules 37 and 50] for you to settle. Either rule 37 accepts the question bubble and the top-bar clock as the match, or rule 50 allows a lead-in per stop when a twin half needs one.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 17: '...nobody who was weakest in an earlier decision sits in a later pair.'
verdicts.breaks: Real for Ganga, and the writer marked it. She is the weakest card in D5 (15 hours on her feet, slept 2), then half of D8's pair. The new D3 point is wrong. No D3 card is weakest on both numbers (Sunil is lowest on ward nights, Dinesh on years known), and rule 17 does not define 'weakest' by a single number.
verdicts.fix: With a slip for each scene, keep every weakest card off later pairs. For D3, nothing is needed unless you rule that weakest on one number counts.

verdicts.breaks: The writer marked this. Rajan arrives with a judging note (D1 'moody'), a plain one (D4) and a heavy fact (D6 'lost his job'). verdicts.breaks: Fetching an 80-year-old woman's clothes from her home, which may include her underclothes, is a job many homes give only to a woman. It pulls the third job towards Mumtaz, Ganga or Yasmin. This pull goes the same way as D1's bedside pull, so twin A leans the same side in both halves (see the night-chair entry).

verdicts.breaks: Read as written, the clause is broken many times over, all under the same set's number names. The bible's fixed numbers for each person cannot meet the literal clause, so it needs a ruling.

verdicts.rule: 42 (and a clash with the options file's B3); merges the measure and rules flags

verdicts.breaks: The outcome runs to five beats (2.30 stamp, 2.31 list, 2.32 reaction and reply, 2.33 fixed ending, 2.34 progress), and rule 42 allows two or three. The writer followed the options file's B3, which lists four steps before progress, and did not mark the clash between B3 and rule 42.

Line 1 always reads 'of 6', a target count that rule 43 allows. The rules flag also raised rule 14 here; that part has the same cause and is covered in the rule 14 entry.

verdicts.breaks: Confirmed. The cards that miss a bar are Nagsen (D1, slept 1), Yasmin (D4, on her feet 10 hours) and Ganga (D5, slept 2): two women and one man. verdicts.breaks: The frame point is not a break. Rule 19 stops the two's notes sharing a frame. It does not stop a nudge using a frame its decoy lacks, and rule 20's decoy of the same kind is present in both decisions (a Nani remark beside a Nani remark, a Mausa ji remark beside a Mausa ji remark). The length point depends on how 'longest' is measured, which rule 19 does not say. By words, the longest Hindi note falls on the two in 3 of 8 decisions (counting ties), inside the quarter-to-half range. By letters, it falls on them only in D7, below the floor. Your 23 Oct words ('the longest quotes are the right one') were about how long a note looks. No open question covers this, so it should go to you as a new one.

With the clock counted, D1 has 17 words in Hindi, D5 16 in English, D6 16 in English and 17 in Hindi, and D8 16 in Hindi. If the English key glosses ('hours on their feet today') show on screen, English decisions run to 16 to 22 words before the button. This depends on whether top-bar text counts, which no question yet settles; it belongs beside question 14.
verdicts.fix: Settle whether the top bar counts. Write the key in the same short words in both languages, and shorten the clocks (for example 'X-ray, 7:30 am' | 'सुबह 7:30, एक्स-रे').

verdicts.beat: 2.07 (D1, Nani voices the nudge on her own bedside)

Neither is a reason that truly matters in rule 20's sense, and rule 16 says nothing about the note of the twin member who carries no nudge.

verdicts.breaks: Rule 51 as written is met: three kinds (Split, Pick one, Spend checks), two of them new, and no clause bars a kind twice in a row. verdicts.breaks: No break as written. Rule 21 balances marked names across pairs, decoys and top and bottom places, not what the notes say. Rule 1 is the 'I have lived this' test. verdicts.breaks: 'Half' (आधी) is a common quantifier, and the line says nothing about Uma or Dinesh. The empty corridor behind Mausa ji, and his face-on look (rule 7 wants people to look out at you), break no rule.

The build counts a card as weakest only when every other card beats it on both numbers, and by that test decision 3 has no weakest card. Francis is last on 'free' (1 day), but Kusum is last on 'km' (10), and their ranks add up to the same total. Against the target on screen (3 days free or more), though, Francis is the only card that misses, and the player can see that. The warmth half of the flag is wrong: 'Driving test next month' is neutral in warmth. That it rules Annamma out is the rule 20 problem, covered in its own entry.
verdicts.fix: Say whether 'weakest' includes 'the only card to miss the target on screen'. If it does, have the build count it, and either take Francis off decision 3 or give decision 3 a different bottom card. Annamma's decision 2 note needs fixing anyway (rule 20 entry).

verdicts.rule_text: Both halves of a twin are asked by the same person, in the same number and shape of bubbles, words within 2, over a lead-in with the same figures and mood. (rule 37) ... a question of at most 10 words and 15 counted words on the screen (rule 63)
verdicts.breaks: Both checkers raised this, so I merged the two flags. 'Who gets the keys to open up at 6 am?' counts 8 words if '6 am' counts as one number, and 9 if 'am' counts, against 6 for decision 8. So 'words within 2' depends on how the counting script treats 'am' after a number, which rule 62's 'numbers' does not settle. The Hindi questions count 8 and 7, which are within 2. Rule 63's 10-word cap for a question holds in both languages. The claim of a 16-word Hindi screen cannot be checked from the beat, which does not list the number names and button on decision 4's screen. The writer's note that every question is 8 words or fewer is wrong in raw words (3.14 in English and 3.22 in Hindi are 10), but no cap is broken.
verdicts.fix: Decide in the counting script whether 'am' and 'pm' count with their number. If the questions in the rule 5 entry are not taken, use 'Who gets the 6 am keys?' | 'सुबह 6 बजे की चाबी किसे मिले?' (4 or 5 counted words in English, 6 in Hindi). Correct the writer's note.

verdicts.rule_text: Before and during a decision, no bubble, caption or sign names, points at, describes, or uses the note words of anyone on that decision's cards (rule 36) ... the title card names the setting plainly before Start (rule 26)
verdicts.breaks: This depends on a call the rulebook leaves open: whether rule 36's 'before ... a decision' reaches the cover. It is a clash between rules 26 and 36, and none of the sixteen questions covers it. Rule 26 requires the cover to name the setting before Start, and the build's own note-word scan starts after the cover. Read that way, the cover is outside rule 36. Read literally, the cover comes before every decision. Its Hindi 'बदसलूकी की शिकायत' matches Vinod's note in decision 4 word for word, and its 'bullying' matches Kavita's English note in decision 8. Even if the cover is exempt, naming the topic points at the card with the hard fact whatever the words; that comes with rule 26 and a hard twin. The 'work' match with Kavita's note in decision 3 is an everyday word and not worth changing.
verdicts.fix: Your call: exempt the cover from rule 36, or not. Either way, break the word-for-word Hindi match by changing one side, for example the note's word, using the Hindi-first readers' choice from the rule 28 entry.

If you say yes to counting speech, the writer counts 97 English and 110 Hindi words (the checker counts 96 and 109), still under 120. The checker reaches 125 and 141 Hindi words only by counting 'Next' and Skip on each of the 16 beats. In the strip design, Next is one pinned button in the bar at the bottom of the screen and Skip sits in the top bar, so counting them on every beat is the checker's assumption, not the rule's.

verdicts.rule_text: The circle goes against type at least as often as with it, judged from an agreed list of typed jobs. (rule 11)
verdicts.breaks: Both checkers raised this, so I merged the two flags. Rule 11 can only be judged from 'an agreed list of typed jobs', and that list does not exist yet (the rule waits on your yes). So the writer's count and the checkers' are both guesses. The checkers' point is fair, though. Most of the women's job notes run against type (truck loading, tiling, house painting, a bottling plant at night). Most of the men's run with it (umbrella repairs, the mill, restoring chairs, a wedding band). 'Dhaba cook' and 'stitches school uniforms' are common men's trades in India, so they may not count as against type. The two Sunday notes on Christian names (football, a wedding band) are ordinary roles under rule 21, so they are not a break. Rohit's 'Cooked years at a dhaba' repeating 'years' breaks nothing: rule 18 says nothing about notes echoing number names.
verdicts.fix: Agree the list of typed jobs. Meanwhile, swap two men's notes for against-type ones (for example 'Knits sweaters for his nieces.') and move one Sunday note off a Christian name. Optionally, change Rohit's note to 'Cooked at a highway dhaba.' (5 words).

Second, Mummy seen from behind appears in seven panels, yet no back-view reference is on the paint list, which the painter's glossary rule asks for anything that recurs. Period dress, flowers in the hair or a pallu over the head are only predictions until the panels are painted.

Add a back-view reference and glossary row for Mummy to the paint list, in positive words (a plain cotton kurta, hair in a low bun), and check each painting. Put Mummy's face chip on her four notes and Masterji's on his four, as the bible's section 4 asks.

verdicts.rule_text: A decision's notes are within 2 words of each other, the equal two's notes are the same length, and the longest note falls on the two in a quarter to a half of decisions.
verdicts.breaks: The checker's figures are right, but they fall inside the rule. In English the longest note falls on the pair in 2 of 8 decisions by words and 3 of 8 by letters (the app's own length check, story_take.length_faults, counts letters and allows at most half). In Hindi it is 4 of 8 by both words and letters: exactly half, the top of the band, which the rule allows. Every pair's two notes have the same number of words in both languages. What remains is your own 23 Oct worry: in both hard decisions, the pair has the two longest notes by letters in both languages, and by words in Hindi.
verdicts.fix: The rule needs no change here. The trims are cheap, though, and worth making with the rule 28 rewrite, as the note-length rule says ('Trim a hard fact to the decision's length rather than padding around it'). For example: 'Complained a past boss bullied workers.' and 'Once complained of bullying by a boss.', with the Hindi trimmed to match. Have the build check letters in Hindi too.

verdicts.rule_text: Every decision has a twin ... the same kind of choice, a different equal two with no shared person, the nudge on the other one, a new place and task, never a near-copy (rule 16) ... A reason that truly matters (holds a driving licence, saw it happen) sits only on the equal two of a "matters" twin (rule 20)
