Each bears on its job to a similar degree: three people clearing mud together, and a counter on the busiest day. Neither is a reason that 'truly matters' in rule 20's sense (a licence, having seen it happen). Rule 16 asks for 'a new place and task', which this has; it does not ask for tasks with the same gender script. Rule 17 does not catch it either: the 'men's work' script sits in one half only, not 'on the same side in both halves'. verdicts.rule_text: Card faces come from the existing portrait library, each keeping one name for good, and every new face passes the close-up check for painted bindis and lightened skin. (rule 33) ... every painting prompt asks for present-day clothes and objects (rule 2)
verdicts.breaks: I checked the library. enamel-francis.webp's prompt asks for 'a white short-sleeved uniform shirt with shoulder straps', and the painting shows the shoulder straps plainly. enamel-annamma.webp's prompt asks for 'a navy uniform shirt', but the painting reads as a plain dark collared shirt, much like Rohit's 'navy work shirt'. So in decision 5 one card stands out, not the pair, and 'the clothes alone give the pair away' is not shown. The library faces are reused with one name each, as rule 33 asks, and a uniform is present-day clothing, so rule 2 holds. On 'Asha': no library face carries that name (Dadi's portrait files are named dadi), the blend's household has no Dadi, and the Asha in people.md belongs to the rejected story. So no face changes its name. What remains is not a rule break: Francis's uniform shows on all five of his cards, hints at a railway job that no note mentions, and in decision 5 sits on the man who carries the nudge.
verdicts.fix: When painting resumes, repaint Francis's Station portrait in plain present-day clothes, run the close-up check, and add it to the chapter's painting list. Raise uniforms on library faces as a surface tell with the research check. Renaming Asha is optional; it would avoid confusion while people.md still holds the old Dadi.

verdicts.rule_text: Each decision shows 3 to 5 people who look alike before a choice, with exactly one woman and one man matched on every number, portraits within 8 years of age and no second woman-and-man tie (rule 13)
verdicts.breaks: Rule 13's 'look alike before a choice' comes from your 21 Oct 'cards that look the same before a choice'. It means no card is marked out, not that each decision mixes women and men. Rule 11 balances the circle, not each decision, and rule 15 is about ties. So no rule is broken. The giveaway is real, though, for a player who knows a woman and a man are hidden: the only man in decision 2, and the only woman in decisions 6 and 8, must be in the pair. It is a surface tell to raise with the research check (RSE-164), as the note-length rule asks, rather than fix silently.
verdicts.fix: Raise it with the research check. If it should become a rule, add to rule 13 for your yes: 'at least two women and two men on a five-card decision, and one of each beside the pair on a four-card one'. Then rerun the search.

verdicts.rule_text: Two everyday numbers per card, named after the task (meals cooked for a crowd, times late this month), the same number names in the same order with one key

'Days free this week' shows 6 for Asha and Vinod at Friday noon and for Sapna on Friday night, when only a day or two of the week is left. It also does not go down for people hired earlier in the week. Mr Natarajan, the persona who keeps to rules, is the player most likely to notice.

The line also stays within rule 35: it gives the month, the place and the state the place is in. The real nit is the picture. One painting serves all three languages (rule 30), and the Hindi's घुटनों तक (knee-deep) sits over water painted 'over her sandals' (3.02) and 'over the step' (3.01).

verdicts.breaks: Both checkers raised this, so I merged the two flags. Neither rule 65 nor any other rule says anything about register. उनके is ordinary respectful Hindi when speaking of a death. The note sits on a decoy, and drawing the eye to a decoy does the measure no harm: the heavy fact is meant to sit on one.

In 3.15, keys hanging on the nail at night read as not handed over.

The bible tags him on every bubble as the chapter's voice. And rule 22 only needs a named speaker with a portrait. The clarity point is fair, though: in Hindi, मास्टरजी more often means a teacher.

verdicts.rule_text: The player speaks to elders politely (लिस्ट दिखाइए, not लिस्ट दो) (rule 66) ... no trade words an outsider would not know ("learned the section", "second XI") (rule 2)
verdicts.breaks: 3.03: rule 66's politeness rule is about Hindi, and the Hindi says दिखाइए; the rulebook's own question 14 has the player say 'Okay. Show the list.'. 3.22: 'haat' is a regional everyday word, not a trade word in rule 2's sense, though Shruti (who grew up in Mysuru) and Mr Natarajan (Coimbatore) may not know it. 3.26: बारिश is everyday Hindi for the rains; बरसात would also do.

verdicts.rule_text: Two everyday numbers per card, named after the task (meals cooked for a crowd, times late this month) (rule 18)
verdicts.breaks: Rule 18's own example of an everyday number is 'times late this month', so 'days late last month' is the kind of number the rule asks for. Whether an applicant would write it on a slip, and how Mummy would know it, is a reader question under rule 1, not a rule 5 break.
verdicts.fix: Optional: 'days worked last month' (more is better) reads more naturally on a slip. If you take it, turn the targets and bars round to match, and rerun build_ch3.py and the outcome check.

verdicts.rule_text: No situation, nudge wording or set of numbers is ever used twice ... a role may come back in a new place with a new nudge.
verdicts.breaks: Rule 6 bans repeating a nudge's wording, and 'Chatty at work' (3.12) differs from chapter 5's 'Talks far too much, all day long' (5.07). Roles may come back in a new place, and rule 25 only limits which decision number the hard twin sits at. Still, this is worth raising with the measure check, as the note-length rule asks for any surface tell. The idea of talking too much is a nudge in chapters 3 and 5 and a decoy note in chapter 2 ('Too chatty, Nani says', 2.07). The phone remark repeats on decoys (3.17, 5.07). 'Lost his job when the mill shut' (3.24) returns almost word for word in 5.19 ('Lost her job when the mill shut in spring'). And the hard twins in chapters 2, 3 and 5 all hang on keys, cash, a purse or a register.
verdicts.fix: Keep 'chatty' here and ask the chapter 5 writer for a different idea. Rewrite one of the two mill lines. The questions in the rule 5 entry move this chapter's hard twin away from keys and cash. Raise the pattern across the take with the measure check rather than fixing it silently.

Rule 13: every decision has exactly one woman-and-man tie, and it is the marked equal two. The two are 0 to 5 years apart.

Rule 14: in all four pick-one decisions, the two lead on each number taken alone. In both team decisions, two cards sit above them on each number, so a one-number player must take one of them for the third place. In both rank decisions they share places 2 and 3 on each number.
Rule 15, second part: the pair is never the top two in a rank or team decision (0 of 4).

Rule 19, words: in every decision the notes are within 2 words of each other in both languages, and the two's notes are the same length in both. The two never share an opening word or a sentence frame. In English the longest note falls on the two in 2 of 8 decisions (alone in decision 7, shared in decision 8).
Rule 16: all four twins keep the same kind, share no person between halves and put the nudge on the other sex. The matters twin's licence notes are new words, not a one-word swap.

Rule 37: the same asker (Mummy) in both halves of every twin, the same number of bubbles (1 and 1, 1 and 1, 1 and 1, 0 and 0) and lead-ins with the same figures. Question words are within 2 for twins A, B and C in both languages, and for twin D in Hindi.

Rule 17, partly: no pair repeats, nobody is in more than two pairs, nobody is in pairs two decisions running, and no pair's exact numbers return as a pair under the same number names. Who is older switches side in twins A and D and never sits on the same side in twins B and C.
Every applicant keeps the same numbers all week within each set (years and late; km and free), which is realistic.

Rule 22: Masterji's and Mummy's judging notes each fall on 2 women and 2 men, and each lands on a decoy beside the nudge. No note speaks about women or men in general, and no gossip touches the hard fact.

Rule 20, partly: every plain decision has a loaded decoy of the nudge's kind. Both hard decisions put a heavy-sounding fact on a decoy with an unmarked name (Kusum, Rohit). The hard fact sits on only one of the two in decisions 4 and 8.

Rules 44 and 45: over all 40,000 answer sets for the four decisions that feed targets, swapping the two never changes the band. Always picking the woman, always the man, going only by the first number and going only by the second all end at 9:00. All three bands can happen (2,304 at 9:00, 16,192 at 9:30, 21,504 at 10:15). Every bar sits at or below the two's numbers (late 2 or fewer, against their 1 and 2; free 3 or more, against their 4 and 5). Cards that miss a bar are 2 women and 2 men. The matters and hard twins change nothing.
Rule 36: no lead-in or question uses a card's note words. The only overlap the script found is 'last' in 'Sun at last' against Asha's 'last summer', which is a different sense.

Rule 62: the story beats total 99 English and 110 Hindi counted words (cap 120). No story beat goes over 20 words or 3 pieces (the title card aside). Every spoken line is 10 words or fewer and every narration 12 or fewer.
Rule 63: every decision screen is 15 counted words or fewer in English. In Hindi all are within 15 except decision 4, which reaches 16 only if the number names count.

Rule 66: no gendered future and no gendered helper verb in any line by, to or about the player. The player's two lines are a polite command and a line with no verb. Every 'who should' question uses the subjunctive. The subjunctives the writer flagged (करे, रहे, मिले, जाए) still wait for a native reader.
Rule 21 inside pairs: both names in a pair are marked (decisions 5 and 7, Christian) or neither is. No card name matches a persona's name.

Rule 25: the hard twin's first half is at decision 4, a position no other chapter uses. Rules 26 and 27: the hard topic never reaches a panel or a bubble, the title card names the setting before Start, and it is an applicant's own past, not the household's.
Rules 7, 32 and 33: the player and the card people are never painted, Mummy is always seen from behind, and Masterji is face-on as the chapter's voice.
Relation words: none mark the pair. The only pronouns on a pair's notes are in decision 8, on both of the two (her, his).
Rule 39: every 'it happened' beat is the same whoever was picked, and the settled plates name nobody.
Twin B's two trips (the tempo to the godown, the scooter to the wholesale market) carry the same kind of men's-work script, so the matters twin tests the licence the same way in both halves.

Rule 7: the player is never painted; 3.03 says no hand reaches out; people look out of the picture (Masterji in 3.02 and 3.28) or things face the viewer (the list, the pen, the key ring); every decision backdrop is people-free.

Rule 8 and owner answer 2: nobody uses bhaiya, didi, beta or any kin word for the player; 'The list is yours' | 'लिस्ट तुम्हारे हाथ में' never makes the player the doer; nothing contradicts a grown-up child of 22 to 30 helping at the family shop.

Rule 66: every Hindi line by or to the player marks no gender. That covers the player's polite command to Mummy (पर्चियाँ दिखाइए), the verbless closing line (अगली बारिश में, पहले रेत की बोरियाँ), every 'who should' ask in the subjunctive (करे, पहुँचाए, मिले, रहे, जाए), Mummy's तुम commands (चुनो, क्रम लगाओ), and the game's आप buttons (चुनें, भेजें, शुरू करें). There is no future form, no -ा/-ी before हूँ or हो, and no sentence-final past. The 10 lines build_ch3.py flags are subjunctives and बजे cases that rule 66 sends to a native reader; none fixes a gender.

Rules 10 and 37: there is one asker (Mummy, a woman, keeping the bible's 3 women and 2 men), never on a card and never the comic one. The hard questions sit in the plain question box. Both halves of every twin are asked by Mummy over matching lead-ins: Mummy from behind before decisions 1 and 5 and before 3 and 7; people-free clock-and-sound beats before 2 and 6 and before 4 and 8. Question lengths are within 2 words in both languages for twins A, B and C.
Rule 22 (measure section, noted only): judging notes come from a woman (Mummy) and a man (Masterji), each on 2 women and 2 men, and none says anything about women or men in general.

Rules 25, 27 and 29: there is one hard topic, and the event really holds it (an applicant's past complaint). It is someone else's case, and the household never does the wrong. The first half sits at decision 4, which no other chapter uses. Station's big moment lands on the event, never on a hard decision. The chapter opens and closes warm. No child is at risk and no court appears. The heavy decoy facts (a husband's death, a mill job lost) sit on Kusum and Rohit, off the equal two.

Rule 26: the paintings behind decisions 4 and 8 show only the shop; no panel, bubble or sound word touches bullying; there are no puns; the cover names the topic before Start (see the clash flagged on 3.01).

Rules 3, 4 and 48: no festival, ritual, prayer, religious symbol, brand, famous person or community-marked place is named; there are no money amounts and no domestic help; the event belongs to no faith, and its goal is one number (Saturday, 9:00, shutter up).

Rules 11 and 12: the circle is 10 applicants, 5 women and 5 men, all the same kind of relation to the household. They are met on 3.05 as names only, over a people-free counter, in a new order on every load. Everyone is 18 or over, in roles open to both.

Rules 32 and 39: no card person is painted; settled plates show a tick, a job word and a lock with no names; every 'it happened' beat is the same for every pick; there is no reply after a pick, so options Q14 does not arise.
Rule 38: there are two 'You' lines, both fixed and the same in every band. They name nobody, give no rule for choosing and agree with no remark.

Rules 43 to 46: two targets in card-number words are handed over at the start, and every decision happens before Saturday 9:00. The stamp follows the numbers only: build_report shows 0 swap differences over every answer, 'always the woman' and 'always the man' both end at 9:00, all three bands can happen, and the cards that miss a bar are 2 women and 2 men. Outcome lines name nobody, praise or blame nobody, and are warm in every band.

Rules 49 to 51: the chapter wears the Station look and keeps its work area, in calendar order (July). It has 8 decisions and 4 twins (two plain, one matters, one hard), with halves four decisions apart and the story clock on every decision. The calendar's pencil circle differs from the red ones by line and shape as well as colour. It uses three kinds (team, pick one, rank), none new.

Rules 62 and 63, counted as the bible counts them. Every story beat (the cover apart) has at most 20 counted words and 3 pieces. Every spoken line is 10 words or fewer (Mummy's Hindi in 3.03 and Masterji's in 3.28 are exactly 10 tokens), and every narration 12 or fewer. verdicts.rule_text: 15. The equal two are never the only tie: from chapter 2 on, at least half the decisions also show two women or two men tied, and in rank, team, batting order and split the equal two are the top two in at most half the decisions.

The writer marked it. The cause is structural. With 10 people, 5 women and 5 men (rule 11), and two number sets (rule 18), each set holds four woman-and-man pairs and leaves exactly one woman and one man free. Two people of one sex can only tie if one copies a pair's numbers, which rule 17's last clause forbids: 'a pair's exact numbers never return under the same number names that chapter'.
verdicts.fix: No fix exists inside the rules as written, so this needs the owner's call. The suggested eleventh lane player breaks rule 11 twice (8 to 10 people, half women and half men), so it is not a free fix. The writer says chapters 2, 3 and 5 already have one, and the owner should see that as a rule 11 exception too. The choices are: let a same-sex tie reuse a pair's numbers (an exception to rule 17's last clause, kept off that pair's own card), or allow one card person who is never in a pair (an exception to rule 11). Lalit is the only person with no pair still to come, so rule 17's weakest-card clause needs him at the bottom of D2. At 8/2 he would top D2 instead. Take him off D2 and the weakest card there would be Mitali, who pairs at D8. If no ten-person layout passes, take it to the owner as options Q8 (one set, 16 to 20 people) or as a named exception to rule 15. Keep the chapter out of playtest until one is chosen.

verdicts.rule_text: Inside a pair, the two match on how they appeared earlier that chapter: on the same number of cards, as high on the numbers each time (both in the top half of those cards, or both in the bottom half), with notes of the same warmth; nobody who was weakest in an earlier decision sits in a later pair.
verdicts.breaks: Before D5, Rekha has one showing (D2: tied top of 4, as one of the equal two, carrying the scooter fact). Gopal has none. The pair fails 'on the same number of cards'. The writer marked [BREAKS rule 17] on 5.17 (note 2). I agree Gopal's set-B 10/1 would top D2 and D3. That leaves him only a bottom-half showing in set A, which still would not match Rekha's top-half one.
verdicts.fix: Answer options Q8, since one larger set lets Gopal show earlier. Until a layout passes, keep twin A (D1, D5) out of reading card 3, which uses plain and matters twins, and tell the readers that D5's reading is soft.

verdicts.rule_text: The equal two really compete for the same place: a player who goes only by the first number, or only by the second, still has to choose between them, and the build refuses any plain or hard decision that fails.
verdicts.breaks: This merges the measure flag and the first half of the rules flag on 42. In src/take/steps/Pick.tsx each tapped card takes one check, a second tap takes it back, at least one is needed ('Take up at least one'), and taps stop at the max. So the need lines' 'one person may carry both' cannot happen. As built, a numbers-only player who spends one check gives it to Sarla (D1) or Naresh (D5) and never chooses between the two. Both halves of twin A fail rule 14 for that player. The 5.07 mark and writer note 19 describe this but do not mark it as a break. The story also leaves the second envelope or key with nobody. The rules checker's fix ('one person may still take both') cannot be built.
verdicts.fix: Ask for two different holders. Either make the step take exactly 2 ('One envelope each' | 'एक-एक लिफ़ाफ़ा'; a build change, since today it accepts 1). Or make D1 and D5 Pick a team, 2 of 4: that kind was met in chapter 1, chapter 5 still has four kinds, and Spend checks is still met at chapter 2's D4 and D8. Either way {n} on 5.26 becomes a fixed 4.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 12: "Everyone on a card, speaking or choosing is 18 or over, in a role a woman or a man could hold in India today that means the same for both". Rule 5: "Ask the player only what someone in their place would really be asked".
verdicts.breaks: This merges the measure and rules flags. The blend's own options file (A4) lists 'jewellery keys' among 'Jobs that carry a gender script', so D6's job does not 'mean the same for both'. A player who follows that script gives Sarla the key, which in this hard twin looks like steering away from the dowry fact on Naresh. Three parts of the flags do not hold. The gift register is not on that list, and its script is a guess. No rule asks both halves to show the same number of cards: rule 13 allows 4 and 5. Whether someone aged 22 to 30 would be asked to place the jewellery key (rule 5) is for the six-player readers under rule 1.
verdicts.fix: Give D6 a trust job with no script, keeping 5.18's lead-in and the padlock painting: 'Who keeps the key to the guests' bag room?' | 'मेहमानों के सामान वाले कमरे की चाबी कौन रखे?' (9 and 9 counted, within 2 of D2). If a second key straight after D5's keys feels repetitive, use a non-key job of the register's weight. Put both jobs to the five Hindi-first readers with the scooter pair.

verdicts.beat: 5.15 (D4 front row) and 5.24 (D8 cake), plain twin D
verdicts.rule_text: "in a plain twin the nudge should not matter (a loaded word)"; rule 16: "the same kind of choice, a different equal two with no shared person, the nudge on the other one, a new place and task, never a near-copy (no one-word swap, no her-to-his swap)."
verdicts.breaks: This merges the measure and rules flags. D4's 'Far too modern for the old folks.' names elders on a job that means sitting beside 80-year-old Nani, so the plain nudge bears on the task. D8 carries a different, milder idea ('Has no patience at all for old ways'), not the same nudge on the other person. In Hindi, मॉडर्न said of a woman is the loaded word; चिढ़ है is not. Two of the measure's points do not hold. No rule asks partner deeds to match in type: the with-type deed sits on the un-nudged partner in both halves, not on one gender. 'Sitting beside Nani reads as care' is a guess for the readers.
verdicts.fix: Use one loaded idea, 'too modern', in both halves, with no elders, in new frames (not a her-to-his swap), each matched to the partner card's length. D4 Sarla: 'Far too modern, in my honest view.' | 'मेरी राय में तो कुछ ज़्यादा ही मॉडर्न।' (7 and 8, as Satish). D8 Tapan: 'Acts far more modern than he ever should.' | 'जितना चाहिए, उससे ज़्यादा मॉडर्न बनता है।' (8 and 7, as Mitali). Rerun the measure check, then send both to the five Hindi-first readers.

verdicts.beat: 5.09 (D2) and 5.19 (D6), the scooter pair of hard twin B
verdicts.rule_text: A hard fact means the same for a woman and a man: "bullying", not "harassment", at work, and "refused to give dowry" against "took no dowry" fails; every hard pair is read by the five Hindi-first players before it ships.
verdicts.breaks: This merges the measure flag with the in-laws point in the rules flag. The two facts do not describe the same act. Rekha 'Turned down a scooter demand when her niece married': at the wedding, a demand, ठुकराई (spurned). Naresh 'His niece's in-laws asked for a scooter; he refused': ससुराल, after the marriage, a request, मना किया (said no). A demand from a married niece's in-laws reads closer to dowry harassment, and spurning a demand is the stronger act. The bible put both at a niece's wedding, and D6 drifted from it. The five-reader mark stays, but the gap already shows in the words.
verdicts.fix: Put both at a past wedding with a time word and the groom's side as the one asking (लड़के वाले, never ससुराल). Use 'no scooter' or 'demand' (माँग) in both, verbs of equal weight, different frames (rule 16) and 9 counted words to match the partner card. D2: 'Years back, she told a groom's side: no scooter.' D6: 'Said no to a groom's scooter demand, years ago.' Write Hindi of the same shape (बरसों/सालों पहले, लड़के वाले, मना किया). Avoid शादी and 'wedding', which are on the title card (rule 36). Then ask the five readers both 'same weight?' and 'is this about this wedding?'.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 31: "close-ups only for one short line, two or three people a panel at most". Rule 3: "No ritual, prayer, religious dress, religious or political symbol, real brand, famous person or community-marked place on screen or in a painting prompt."
verdicts.breaks: Each prompt asks for a crowd: small dark shapes of guests (5.10), chairs filling with guests (5.20), sixty guests at long tables (5.25), guests' heads around Nani (5.28). That is against 'two or three people a panel at most', and none is marked. A crowd is where FLUX adds forehead marks and faith-marked dress. 5.20's 'no ritual object, no dress that marks a faith' puts those very words into the prompt. The owner's painter-glossary rule forbids that: 'Definitions say what to paint, never what not to paint'.
verdicts.fix: Show the event through things, with at most two or three far figures: 5.10, bags and rolled quilts set down under the newly lit bulbs, the bus gone; 5.20, rows of chairs with shawls and handbags left on them; 5.25, long tables of sixty steel plates with steam rising; 5.28, Nani's back, her cane and the cake. If the owner wants crowds, mark each [BREAKS rule 31], describe the clothes in positive words, and run the close-up check on every crowd panel.

verdicts.beat: Chapter 5 as a whole (5.03 to 5.28; 5.14, 5.21, 5.25 most exposed)
verdicts.rule_text: A First take event, and every decision in it, passes only if real people like each of our six players say "I have lived this, or watched it at home"; the writer's own guess does not count.
verdicts.breaks: Under rule 1 neither the writer nor a checker can pass or fail this; only the readers can. The four risks are fair predictions: a brass band read as the groom's side's, the unnamed stage evening read as a sangeet, a birthday cake on the wedding night, and dinner for only sixty. Writer note 20 names the band and the Coimbatore and Bengaluru players, but no beat carries a wait mark. This depends on the six-player readers, not on an owner question.
verdicts.fix: Mark 5.14, 5.21 and 5.25 [WAITS rule 1: six-player readers] and send the chapter to the Coimbatore and Bengaluru stand-ins first. Keep the swaps ready (a sound man for the band, 'the family dinner' for Friday, 'Sixty house guests fed') and use them only when a reader fails a beat.

verdicts.rule_text: A hard topic arrives as someone else's case the player weighs (a neighbour's report, a cousin's complaint), never the player's own life or the household's, and the household is never the one doing the wrong.
verdicts.breaks: Mama ji's daughter is the bride, and the circle are relatives from Mummy's side (bible section 12), so she is a niece to everyone on the cards. D6's 'His niece's in-laws asked for a scooter; he refused.' gives no time, and ससुराल can name her new in-laws. On the Friday night many players may read it as this wedding's groom's side asking Mama ji's family, which is the household's own case. Strict English points the other way: a niece who has in-laws is already married, and D2's 'when her niece married' is plainly past. So it is not a plain break. It depends on the five Hindi-first readers and on options Q3 ('Can a hard topic touch the family's own?'), and the beats' marks treat Q3 as answered. Severity is lowered from blocks because the literal text is a past case and the fix is a few words.
verdicts.fix: Remove the doubt now with the rule 28 drafts above: past tense, a time word, the groom's side as लड़के वाले, no 'his/her niece'. Ask the five readers 'is this about this wedding?'. Change 5.09's and 5.19's marks to [WAITS options Q3] instead of saying rule 27 is met.

verdicts.rule_text: The chapter opens with a short list of targets as a time, a count or a sum (everyone fed by 1, 40 plates, within one week's spending); every decision feeds one target or none and happens before the outcome in story time; the outcome stamps each target, and the number met falls in one of three bands set in advance (on time, a bit late, a rough night).
verdicts.breaks: This merges the measure and rules flags. D8 is asked at 8:00, before the 9:00 dinner the stamp times. The job it decides, carrying the cake out 'After dinner' (5.23, 5.28, writer note 9), happens after that dinner, so a player cannot see how it made dinner late. The rule's 'happens before the outcome in story time' does not say whether it means the moment of asking (the story clock) or the job. The writer read it as the asking. The judges' fix the rule came from was about the job (the strip's '5:15 train' after the 1:00 lunch). This is a rulebook wording point, not a listed question. The D4 part is wrong: Friday's seats are a thin cause for Saturday's dinner, but no rule text asks for a causal link.
verdicts.fix: Write into rule 43 that the job's story time falls before the outcome. Then give D8 a job of the same honour before 9:00, such as walking Nani in to dinner at 8:30, with its question within 2 words of D4's, and keep the cake in the fixed ending. Or stamp the cake's time ('Nani's cake: 10:00 | 10:30 | 11:15') and rewrite Mama ji's band lines to match.

verdicts.rule_text: It gives only the goal of the moment ("The mandi shuts at eleven"), never the number the two tie on. Both halves of a twin are asked by the same person, in the same number and shape of bubbles, words within 2, over a lead-in with the same figures and mood.
verdicts.breaks: Twin C's Hindi questions are 5 counted words (डिब्बों पर किसकी बात मानें?) and 8 (बैंड के पैसों पर किसकी बात सही मानें?). They are 3 apart, against 'words within 2'. The English questions are 8 and 8. The सही half of the flag is wrong: सही मानें is the everyday way to say 'believe', and the rule bars stating the tie, not this verb. The two tie on both numbers anyway. Severity is lowered because the overage is one word, in one language.
verdicts.fix: 'बैंड के पैसों पर किसका यक़ीन करें?' (7 counted, within 2 of D3), or lengthen D3 to 'मिठाई के डिब्बों पर किसकी बात मानें?' (7).

verdicts.rule_text: The outcome comes only after the chapter's last pick, in two or three beats: one painting of the event with the result laid on as live text in the world's own stamp, the asker's reaction with the player's fixed reply, then progress and Next chapter; never a row or a count of the player's picks.
verdicts.breaks: This merges the measure flag and the second half of the rules flag on 42. The {n} in 'Envelopes and keys ... {k}/{n}' is the number of different people the player gave envelopes and keys to (1 to 4 as built). That makes it a count of the player's picks, which the rule rules out. Chapter 1's list uses a fixed 'of 4'. The '{k}/4' line for front row and cake matches chapter 1's '4 of 4' and counts places that met the bar. That line waits only on Q5 and options Q15, as chapter 1's does.
verdicts.fix: Once D1 and D5 take two different holders (the rule 14 fix), stamp 'Envelopes and keys, 4 slips or fewer: {k} of 4', as chapter 1 does. Leave the fixed-denominator form to the owner's Q5 and options Q15.

verdicts.rule_text: Decoys are the same kind as the nudge: every decision has at least one card outside the equal two with a note of the nudge's kind (a family worry beside a family worry).
verdicts.breaks: Rules 19 and 36 do not cover this. Rule 19 compares only the two's own notes, and rule 36 covers bubbles, captions and signs, not card notes. The tell falls under rule 20. D6's nudge is a family matter (a niece's in-laws), and no card outside the two carries a family note: the heavy decoy is a work loss (Rekha's mill job). D2 kept 'a family worry beside a family worry' with Lalit's father.
verdicts.fix: Give the heavy decoy a family word of the same weight: Rekha 'Lost her job at her uncle's mill this spring.' (9 words, as now), with Hindi to match. Rerun the length check.

verdicts.rule_text: Before and during a decision, no bubble, caption or sign names, points at, describes, or uses the note words of anyone on that decision's cards ("Pune", "the baby"); decoys stay as card notes, not bubbles.
verdicts.breaks: This merges the measure and rules flags. 'Late bus guests need their rooms.' | 'आख़िरी बस वालों को कमरे चाहिए।' uses 'late' and 'bus' (बस) from Lalit's D4 note 'Got in late on Wednesday night, by bus.' | 'बुधवार को देर रात बस से पहुँचा।'. Lalit is on D5's cards. The writer's scan checked each note against the bubbles before it, so a later bubble repeating an earlier note slipped through. It points at the weakest card, a decoy, not at the two, so polish rather than weakens.
verdicts.fix: 'The last guests need their rooms.' | 'आख़िरी मेहमानों को कमरे चाहिए।'. Widen the scan to every note a card person has carried earlier in the chapter.

verdicts.rule_text: Before and during a decision, no bubble, caption or sign names, points at, describes, or uses the note words of anyone on that decision's cards ("Pune", "the baby"); decoys stay as card notes, not bubbles.
verdicts.breaks: The question in Mama ji's bubble, 'Who carries Nani's cake out tonight?', uses 'carry', the word in Dolly's D8 note 'Carried both gas cylinders up the stairs.', during the decision. This is English only; the Hindi shares nothing. The rule 20 part is wrong: lifting cylinders is not a reason that truly matters for carrying a cake.
verdicts.fix: Dolly: 'Swept the whole terrace clean before lunch.' (7 words, as now; Hindi to match). The same scan should also catch D1's 'Who carries the two advance envelopes?', which comes before Mitali's D2 note 'Carried the steel plates up from the station.'

verdicts.rule_text: Before and during a decision, no bubble, caption or sign names, points at, describes, or uses the note words of anyone on that decision's cards ("Pune", "the baby"); decoys stay as card notes, not bubbles.
verdicts.breaks: The title card's 'talk of a dowry' is a sign shown before D1. It shares 'talk' with Naresh's D1 note 'Talks far too much, all day long.', and Naresh carries the dowry fact at D6. This is English only. The title line must name the setting (rule 26), so the note should change, not the card.
verdicts.fix: Naresh: 'Goes on and on, morning to night.' (7 words, as now). This also stays clear of chapter 3's 'chatty'. The Hindi is unchanged.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 31: "close-ups only for one short line". Rule 40: "a painted phone or sign under 60% of the panel becomes a message card below".
verdicts.breaks: 5.04 is painted 'Waist up, close' yet carries the 13-word target sign plus your line, against 'close-ups only for one short line'. The rule 40 parts are not breaks: the move to a message card happens by itself and needs no mark. At 5.25, though, the oval sits in the upper third. By rule 40 the stamp then drops under the picture, and Jadugar's cloth sweeps away to an empty oval, which loses the world's big moment (rule 2). Not stating 5.26's size breaks nothing.
verdicts.fix: Paint 5.04 as a mid shot with the list held large in the foreground, or mark the rule 40 fallback as 5.02 does. Centre 5.25's oval at 60% or more of the picture. Say that 5.26's list fills the panel.

verdicts.beat: 5.25 to 5.28, and the missing album button
verdicts.rule_text: The outcome comes only after the chapter's last pick, in two or three beats: one painting of the event with the result laid on as live text in the world's own stamp, the asker's reaction with the player's fixed reply, then progress and Next chapter; never a row or a count of the player's picks.
verdicts.breaks: Four outcome beats follow the last pick (5.25 stamp, 5.26 list, 5.27 reaction, 5.28 fixed ending), against 'two or three beats'. Chapter 1 marks the same break at 1.41 ('[BREAKS rule 42: five beats ...]'); chapter 5 marks nothing. Progress appears only as a mark on 5.28. The button that opens the album has no words, so it is missing from the counted words. The rule 40 part is weak: read without pictures, 5.27's 'Now, Nani's cake.' carries 5.28's 'After dinner.'
verdicts.fix: Mark 5.25 [BREAKS rule 42: four beats, since rule 43 adds the list and the bible adds the fixed ending], as chapter 1 does. Add a closing beat with the full calendar and the album button ('The album' | 'एल्बम'), counted with the outcome beats.

verdicts.rule_text: Every line is written for Hinglish (the default), Hindi in Devanagari and English
verdicts.breaks: Rule 35 only lists sound words as a kind, so it is not broken. But the English sound word 'paan' names the betel leaf, not a horn, and it does not say what the Hindi पों says. The English line is wrong for English.
verdicts.fix: 'pon' | 'पों', or 'peep' | 'पीं'.

verdicts.rule_text: Card faces come from the existing portrait library, each keeping one name for good, and every new face passes the close-up check for painted bindis and lightened skin.
verdicts.breaks: Writer note 15 needs ten Jadugar faces in present-day clothes. Two are new (Rekha and Satish, already among the bible's eight new faces). Eight are repaints of library faces: Shampa (Rukavat, with a bindi), Tapan (planned in Station) and six troupe faces in stage costume. Rule 2's present-day clothes and rule 13's look-alike cards force the repaints, so these faces do not 'come from the existing portrait library'. That is eight paintings the bible's count leaves out, and 5.05 does not mark it. Severity is lowered because this touches production, not the story or the reading.
verdicts.fix: Mark 5.05 [BREAKS rule 33: eight repaints, forced by rules 2 and 13] for the owner. Or build this circle from library faces already painted in plain present-day clothes. Every repainted face goes through the heavy queue and gets the close-up check.

verdicts.rule_text: A story beat carries at most 20 counted words in at most 3 pieces of text
verdicts.breaks: Five pieces of text, against three. The beat already marks [BREAKS rule 62]. The only new point, that chapter 1's card (1.07) has four pieces, is a consistency gap, not a rule.
verdicts.fix: Match chapter 1 by joining 'About 4 minutes · Start' | 'लगभग 4 मिनट · शुरू करें' into one piece. Ask the owner once to exempt the fixed chapter card in all five chapters.

verdicts.beat: 5.07 to 5.24 (weakest cards; Mitali, Shampa, Tapan; Lalit's remarks)
verdicts.rule_text: Inside a pair both names mark the same community or neither does, and community-marked names sit in pairs, on decoys, at the top and at the bottom as often as their share.
verdicts.breaks: The three Bengali names are 3 of 10 people but the weakest card 0 of 8 times, against 'at the bottom as often as their share' (about 2 of 8). Writer note 8 says so, but no beat is marked. It can be fixed: after D3, Shampa has no pair left, so she could be the weakest card later without breaking rule 17, though not on hard D6 under the people file's no-hard-fact rule. The tone point breaks no rule. Rule 22 allows judging notes from a named voice, and rule 17 forces Lalit to the bottom of D1 to D5.
verdicts.fix: In the rerun pair search, let one Bengali name be the weakest card once (Shampa, off D6). Turn one of Lalit's two Mami remarks into a plain fact, then rerun the rule 17 warmth check and the rule 20 decoy check.

verdicts.rule_text: every relation word gets a plain English label the first time ("Bua, the family's aunt"), checked by a South Indian reader.
verdicts.breaks: 'Mami, Mama ji's wife' carries its plain label, so the beat does what it can. Whether 'maami' reads as marking a caste for a Tamil player is for the South Indian reader the rule names, and that check has not been done.
verdicts.fix: Put 'Mami' to the South Indian reader together with 'Mama ji' and 'Nani'. If it marks a caste, tag her 'Mama ji's wife' and make your line 'Let's see.' | 'दिखाइए।'.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 65: "loaded words sound said of a woman and not of a man in Hindi too"; rule 16: "the nudge on the other one".
verdicts.breaks: The English pair is matched ('Talks far too much', 'Chats for hours'). In Hindi, Rekha's गप्पें लड़ाती है is an idiom said of women, while Naresh's ज़रूरत से कहीं ज़्यादा बोलता है is plain, so the halves carry different loads. Rule 65's clause can be read as wanting the heavier idiom in both halves or in neither. That call belongs to the five Hindi-first readers.
verdicts.fix: Bring both halves to one register, for example Rekha 'जो भी मिले, उससे घंटों बतियाती रहती है।' (8 counted, as Gopal). Avoid बात, which is on the title card. Put the pair to the five readers.

verdicts.rule_text: as high on the numbers each time (both in the top half of those cards, or both in the bottom half)
verdicts.breaks: I recomputed the earlier showings. Dolly: D1 tied 2nd of 4 (top), D4 4th of 5 (bottom). Gopal: D5 tied 2nd of 4 (top), D6 3rd of 5 (the middle card). The pair matches only if the middle card of five counts as bottom half, and the rule does not say. This depends on settling the rule's wording, not on a listed question.
verdicts.fix: Write into rule 17 where the middle card of an odd count sits, and whether 'each time' means in order or as a count. Make check.py use that reading.

verdicts.beat: D1 to D8 (each person's fixed numbers)
verdicts.rule_text: No pair ever repeats, a person is in at most two equal pairs a chapter and never two decisions running, and a pair's exact numbers never return under the same number names that chapter.
verdicts.breaks: Read literally, the rule breaks every time a pair member shows again: Dolly's 8/3 at D4 and D8, Naresh's 8/3 at D5, Rekha's 6/3 at D6 and D7, Tapan's 8/2 at D6 and D7. Read as 'no later pair reuses them', it passes, since none does. The blend's own premise (options A4: 'A person keeps the same numbers wherever a label shows') makes the literal reading impossible for anyone who appears again after their pair. It depends on how the owner settles options Q8 and this wording.
verdicts.fix: Reword the clause as 'no later pair uses an earlier pair's exact numbers under the same number names'. That keeps fixed numbers per person, the honest story choice.

verdicts.rule_text: Every decision says whether being picked is a gain (the seat, the trip) or a load (the 2 am shift): a load is asked as a split or marked as a chore in the game, and unless all five players asked agree which it is, it stays out of the twins.
verdicts.breaks: This merges the measure and rules flags. Each decision says gain or load, so the first clause is met. But the rule keeps a decision out of the twins 'unless all five players asked agree which it is', and every decision here is in a twin, so all eight wait on the five players, not only D2. Some framings make a load plausible: 5.16 has the key-holder waiting up for the late guests, and the envelopes are an errand. This depends on the five players, not on an owner question.
verdicts.fix: Mark D1, D4, D5, D6 and D8 [WAITS rule 23] and put all eight to the five players at once. Or reword 5.16 so the key-holder is not the one waiting up.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 62: "a chapter's story beats total at most 120 words ... Until you answer question 14, your rule stands: speech is left out of the count and a spoken line has no cap." Rule 63: "a question of at most 10 words and 15 counted words on the screen".
verdicts.breaks: Under the owner's standing rule (speech not counted until Q14), the chapter is well under; the 120 cap binds only if Q14 is answered yes. The bubble spec (section 8) counts 'buttons, Skip and Next' without saying once a chapter or once a beat. Counted once, the Hindi reaches 122. If the story clock's day word (शुक्रवार) counts, D4's Hindi screen goes from 15 to 16, over the owner's 15. This depends on Q14 and on how the counter treats the dock and the clock.
verdicts.fix: Put the dock and the clock to the owner with Q14. Meanwhile save two Hindi words (the 5.16 fix saves one) and shorten D4 to 'नानी के पास आगे कौन बैठे?' (5 counted, within 2 of D8's 7).

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 15: "in rank, team, batting order and split the equal two are the top two in at most half the decisions." Rule 18: "Two everyday numbers per card, named after the task ... on a range wide enough (say 0 to 20) to tie two people without a stray second tie."
verdicts.breaks: No cited rule is broken. Rule 14 holds (the flag says so), rule 15's cap is met (top two in 0 of 2 rank decisions), and rule 18 does not ask the two numbers to disagree. The pattern itself is real: writer note 4 says the numbers never disagree, and the pair is always tied at the top or just under one dominant card. The blend's sample checklist (options A4, 'The shapes repeated') asks for the pair's place to vary in rank decisions, so the fix is still worth folding into the rule 15 rerun.
verdicts.fix: In the rule 15 rerun, give each set one decoy whose numbers disagree, and put the two at places 3 and 4 in one of D4 and D8. No rule mark.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 20: "A reason that truly matters (holds a driving licence, saw it happen) sits only on the equal two of a "matters" twin, one a chapter in the First take, never on a decoy."
verdicts.breaks: Neither rule asks the un-nudged partner's account to weigh the same in both halves. Rule 16 is met (the reason sits on Tapan, then on Dolly), and rule 20 is met (the reason that matters sits only on the two). The flag also overstates D3. Shampa's 'on this very shelf at eight' says where the tins were, not where they went, so only Tapan's account answers the question. A player who follows the reason takes Tapan, then Dolly, as a matters twin intends.
verdicts.fix: Optional tightening: give the un-nudged partner a habit or hearsay in both halves, for example Shampa 'Sweets here always go to the cool room.' (8 words). No mark needed.

verdicts.rule_text: Decoys are the same kind as the nudge: every decision has at least one card outside the equal two with a note of the nudge's kind (a family worry beside a family worry).
verdicts.breaks: Each decision has its decoy of the nudge's kind: Lalit's phone and his sleeping (both Mami's remarks), and Dolly's arguing (Mama ji's). The rule says nothing about how strong that card is. The tell is a fair point, but it is not this rule. Moving a remark onto the strongest card also changes rule 17's warmth history.
verdicts.fix: Optional, with the rule 15 rerun: put one decoy remark on the strongest card, as D8 does with Shampa, and rerun the rule 17 warmth check.

verdicts.rule_text: Before and during a decision, no bubble, caption or sign names, points at, describes, or uses the note words of anyone on that decision's cards ("Pune", "the baby"); decoys stay as card notes, not bubbles.
verdicts.breaks: This merges the measure flag and the rules flag on word forms. 'unpaid' (5.21) and 'paid' (Tapan's D7 note) are different words, not two forms of one word as 'carries' and 'Carried' are. In a Believe decision every account has to answer the claim the asker states, and the Hindi shares nothing (आधा बाक़ी against कुछ हिस्सा मिल गया था). '5.18 Upstairs.' places Mama ji before D6. It is a different word from Dolly's 'up the stairs', and her card comes three decisions later. Neither line names, points at or describes a card person.
verdicts.fix: Optional: 'The band says half is still owed.' keeps even the root apart. Settle in rule 36 whether word forms count; if they do, scan stems.

verdicts.rule_text: In the First take, at most two sets of number names a chapter plus one for decisions about a report, whose numbers bear on it (times proved right), and at most about 8 sets in the whole take
verdicts.breaks: Chapter 5 uses two sets in all, inside the 'at most two sets', so set B may score any decision, report or not. 'Times their account proved right' and 'times late this week' also bear on keeping a register and a key.
verdicts.fix: None needed. The bible can drop the label calling set B 'rule 18's set for decisions about a report'.

verdicts.rule_text: Panels are painted with no words in them: signs, papers and screens are painted blank or shown shut, and every word is live text laid on top ... A text check refuses any panel with stray letters unless you allow it with a reason, and your eye is the last check.
verdicts.breaks: The chapter's look line already tells the painter 'No letters anywhere; every surface that would carry writing is painted blank'. Rule 30's text check catches stray letters after painting, and no prompt names a brand (rule 3). The risk is real for a bus's back, a band's drum head and a cake's icing, and the owner's painter-glossary rule wants recurring objects defined in positive words. But nothing in the text breaks the rule.
verdicts.fix: Add glossary rows in positive words before painting: a bus seen from behind, painted one flat cream with a plain yellow number plate (or no bus, only the luggage); a bass drum with a plain crimson head; a plain round cake with smooth white icing and one candle; a plain iron padlock; a two-burner stove on a table.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 2: "no trade words an outsider would not know ("learned the section", "second XI")".
verdicts.breaks: 'Slips' meaning small mistakes is plain English, not a trade word, and rule 65 does not touch it. The clash is real across the take, though: the bible uses 'slips' for the ward's visitor slips (chapter 2), the applicants' slips (chapter 3) and the cricket slips (chapter 4), and here the word sits on a list about envelopes.
verdicts.fix: Use 'mix-ups' in English, with Hindi चूक unchanged: 'Envelopes and keys: 4 mix-ups or fewer.' The word count stays the same.

verdicts.rule_text: met together as their card faces with names only (faces at least 56 px, names at body size), in a new order each time.
verdicts.breaks: The beat asks for 56 px faces and body-size names, as rule 11 requires, and rule 31 governs what is painted, not the live insets. The arithmetic is right: two rows of five faces with names take roughly 160 to 180 px of a 328 x 246 px panel, so the beat's own 'top half' calm space cannot hold them. That is a layout fix, not a break.
verdicts.fix: Paint the canopy roof as calm space over about three-quarters of the picture, or set the ten faces as a grid under the painting.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 7: "The player is never painted, not even a hand, a sleeve or a shadow: people look out of the picture at them and hold things out towards them". Rule 33: "In a world's panels they are seen from behind or speak from off the panel, always with a name tag."
verdicts.breaks: Rule 33 tells the household to appear from behind in a world's panels, so Mama ji from behind is what the rulebook asks, and rule 7's core (the player is never painted) holds. Options Q11 offers the owner other ways, but an open option is not a broken rule.
verdicts.fix: The chapter-level [WAITS options Q11] on 5.03 is enough. Offer the owner the off-panel voice with the umbrella's handle in frame as the other choice.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 33: "always with a name tag. Recurring objects (the list, the keys) are painted from one reference picture." Rule 37: "over a lead-in with the same figures and mood."
verdicts.breaks: Rule 33 identifies a household member by a name tag, not by an object, so a missing umbrella breaks nothing. Rule 37 asks twin lead-ins for 'the same figures and mood', and 5.08 and 5.18 both show Mama ji alone, from behind, in the left third. The umbrella on 5.08 but not on 5.18, and the step pose, are small differences within one twin.
verdicts.fix: Optional: put the umbrella on his arm in every panel he is in, and paint 5.18 with him standing on the landing as in 5.08.

verdicts.rule_text: It never blames anyone, never says right, wrong, fair, failed or well done, never praises one card person and never proves a note true or false.
verdicts.breaks: 'Band: settled.' is the bible's own fixed line. It says the bill ended up cleared, which fits every account: Dolly paid in full, the canopy man settled, part was paid and the rest later, or the band's claim was the usual one. It proves no note true or false. The English does echo Gopal's 'settles up', which a player who picked him may hear as agreement.
verdicts.fix: Optional: reword Gopal's note without 'settle' (9 words, to match Dolly), or use 'Band: playing.' | 'बैंड: चालू।'.

verdicts.rule_text: progress is a story object that fills by decision, told apart by shape as well as colour, with "Chapter 1 of 5" in figures
verdicts.breaks: The rule asks for a story object that fills by decision; it does not say where the object hangs. The continuity slip is real: chapter 1 (1.02) puts the shop calendar on the household's own kitchen wall, and 5.02 hangs it on 'Nani's kitchen wall'.
verdicts.fix: Use 'Our kitchen wall at home', with Mama ji's card tucked into the corner, in both 5.02 and 5.30.

verdicts.rule_text: No ritual, prayer, religious dress, religious or political symbol, real brand, famous person or community-marked place on screen or in a painting prompt.
verdicts.breaks: The prompts ask for 'plain cotton salwar suit, bare forehead' and name no mark of faith, so the text meets rule 3. Red in the hair parting or a black-bead necklace on a married woman is a painting risk. The bible's portrait line already lists sindoor, while rule 33's check names only bindis and lightened skin.
verdicts.fix: Describe Mami's look in positive words ('hair in a plain low bun, a thin plain gold chain'), and widen the close-up check to the hair parting and the neck for Mami and Nani.

verdicts.rule_text: The circle goes against type at least as often as with it, judged from an agreed list of typed jobs.
verdicts.breaks: The rule sets a floor, and the plain facts run 9 against type to 4 with it, so it is met. The skew is real (women 7 of 8 against type, men 2 of 5), but no rule asks for balance between women and men. Lalit's two remarks are judging notes, which rule 22 allows, not quirks.
verdicts.fix: Optional, for players who quit over one-sided framing: give two women with-type or neutral jobs (the Dolly swap in the D8 fix does one) and one more man an against-type job, then rerun the warmth and length checks.

verdicts.beat: 5.07 and 5.17 (twin A); 5.09 and 5.19 against other chapters
verdicts.rule_text: No situation, nudge wording or set of numbers is ever used twice, and a record of every one used lets the build refuse a repeat; a role may come back in a new place with a new nudge.
verdicts.breaks: 'Talks far too much' and 'Chats for hours' are new wording, not chapter 3's 'chatty'. The rule also lets 'a role ... come back in a new place with a new nudge', so keeper jobs in the hard twins of chapters 2, 3 and 5 are allowed. Hard decisions are already marked out by the plain question box (rule 37), so the job pattern gives little away.
verdicts.fix: Optional: give twin A a loaded idea no other chapter uses (for example 'nags' | 'टोकती रहती है'), and vary one hard twin's job across the take.

verdicts.rule_text: Each chapter is painted in a different world and keeps that world's area of life (Station work, Lugdi safety and justice, Jadugar trust, Cricket teams and leaders, Rukavat home and family), and the results read areas by world.
verdicts.breaks: The rule ties the chapter to its world's area, not each decision, and six of the eight decisions are plainly about trust. Two honours read as trust is a fair note for the reading cards, but the text does not break the rule.
verdicts.fix: Optional: note it for the reading cards, or make twin D's jobs trust jobs when D8 is reworked for rule 43.

verdicts.rule_text: Rule 2: "no props from a past era unless the story owns them (the household's old TV), every painting prompt asks for present-day clothes and objects". Rule 48: "five different everyday events that belong to no faith (no festival, named or not ...)".
verdicts.breaks: None of the three is a past-era prop or a festival in the text. 5.20 is captioned 'The wedding day.', and strings of lights at a wedding belong to the event. 'Bedrolls' has two meanings (today's rolled bedding, or the old canvas holdall), and the owner's painter-glossary rule asks for such words to be defined. A steel counter is also odd for a home kitchen.
verdicts.fix: Write 'bags and rolled quilts' (5.10), drop the paper lanterns and keep the bulb strings (5.20), and write 'the kitchen's stone counter' (5.23).

Rule 13: every decision has 4 or 5 cards, the two tied on both numbers, no second woman-and-man tie, and portraits within 8 years (the largest gap is 7, Dolly 33 and Naresh 40).

Rule 14: in all four Pick one and Believe decisions (D2, D3, D6, D7) the two are tied alone at the top on each number, so a first-number-only or second-number-only player must choose between them. In both rank decisions (D4, D8) one card is better and the two share the next place on each number. Checks pass only for a player who spends both checks (see flag).
Rule 15, second part: the two are never the top two in a rank decision (0 of 2).

Rule 16: in each twin both halves are the same kind, with a different pair and no shared person, a new place and task, and the nudge on the other gender (A man then woman, B woman then man, C man then woman, D woman then man). The nudges share no wording beyond the hard fact's own nouns.

Rule 17: no pair repeats. Nobody is in more than two pairs or in pairs two decisions running. No two pairs share numbers under one set. Nobody who was weakest earlier sits in a later pair (Lalit is never paired; Rekha is weakest only from D6, after her pairs). The older person swaps sides in all four twins. Earlier showings match at D4, D6 and D8, and at D7 if the middle card counts as the bottom half.

Rule 19: in every decision the notes are within 2 words of each other and the two's notes are the same length, in English and in Hindi. The two never share an opening word. The longest note sits only on the two in 3 of 8 decisions in English and 2 of 8 in Hindi, inside the book's quarter-to-half (2 to 4). The English is one over the task's 'at most a quarter'.

Rule 20: every decision has a decoy note of the nudge's kind. Both hard decisions put a heavy-sounding fact on a decoy (Lalit's father, Rekha's job). The reason that truly matters sits only on the two, in the matters twin.
Hard twin: the hard fact sits on exactly one of the two in both halves, never in a bubble or panel. It is a relative's own past, not this wedding's (rules 26 and 27).
Rule 21: the Bengali names pair only with each other (Shampa and Tapan, Mitali and Tapan) and carry no hard fact.
Rule 22: the remarks come from Mami and Mama ji (a woman and a man) and appear on five cards besides the two across the chapter. None says anything about women or men in general.

Twin voices: the nudge giver stays the same between halves (Mami for twin A, Mama ji for twin D), and the matters accounts are in the speaker's own voice in both halves. No bubble speaks about the pair.

Rule 37: Mama ji asks both halves of every twin. Each pair of lead-ins shares the figure from behind in the left third and has two bubbles of the same kinds, within 2 words. The two hard questions sit in the plain question box.

Rules 43 to 45: targets come from the numbers only, and all three stamp bands can happen. Over every legal answer (checks as built, one per card, at least one), swapping the two never changes a target, so 'always the woman' and 'always the man' end the same. Each bar sits at or below its own two, with a stronger card that also meets it. The cards that miss a bar are 3 women and 3 men. The hard twin feeds nothing, and the matters twin has a fixed result.

Rule 66 (read, not scripted): every Hindi line by or to the player shows no gender. The 'who should' asks are subjunctive (कौन ले जाए?, कौन बैठे?, कौन रखे?, कौन लेकर आए?), the buttons are polite plurals, and your lines to elders are polite (दिखाइए, मामी).

Rule 7: you are never painted. The only hand-over is Mami's, in her own hands with her face in the same picture (5.04); envelopes, keys and the list otherwise lie on surfaces. No hand, sleeve or shadow of yours anywhere.
Rule 8 and rulebook Q7: nobody calls you bhaiya, didi, beta or any kin word; you are only 'you'. Nothing gives you an age, gender, caste or faith.

Rule 66: every Hindi line to or from you marks no gender: Mami's command 'तो मेरी लिस्ट तुम सँभालो।', your polite 'दिखाइए, मामी।', and the verbless 'अब, नानी का केक।' and 'अगले साल। यही कैलेंडर।'. Every 'who should' ask is subjunctive (ले जाए, बैठे, रखे, लेकर आए), with no gendered future. Buttons and the title card use आप forms (सौंप दें, बिठाएँ, मानें, शुरू करें). The checker's flags (आएँ, आए, रखे, बैठे, नहीं, रहे, बाक़ी, मामी) all show no gender and wait only on the native reader.
Rule 38: your three lines are fixed, the same in every band. They name no card person and never agree or disagree with a remark, and there is no reply after a pick while options Q14 is open.
Rule 39: the 'it happened' beats (5.10, 5.13, 5.20) are the same for every pick and come only at a change of place or day; settled plates carry no names or faces.

Rules 25, 26 and 29: dowry reaches no panel or bubble except the title card, which names it before Start. Hard-decision backdrops show only the setting. The hard twin's first half sits at D2 in chapters 2 and 5 only. Jadugar's cloth lands on the outcome, never on a hard decision. There is no violence at home, no child and no court, and the heavy decoy facts sit on the weakest cards, off community-marked names.
Rule 28: both hard facts act for a bride's side and use the same relation word (भतीजी); they are marked for the five Hindi-first readers (subject to the timing fix flagged above).

Rules 9, 10 and 37: one asker (Mama ji, a man, never on a card, not the comic one); the household speaks only in its own chapter, with Nani only in the album. Hard asks sit in the plain question box. Each twin's lead-ins have the same figure and two bubbles, with counted words within 2 (English/Hindi: A 9/9 and 9/9; B 7/8 and 6/6; C 8/8 and 8/8 or 9; D 7/7 and 5/6). The asks give only the goal of the moment.
Rule 36: no bubble, caption or sign names a card person or uses a relation word for one. The circle page has no narration, and the D2 note uses ब्याह to keep the title card's शादी off it.
Rule 11: a circle of ten, five women and five men, all relatives from Mummy's side, shown with names only in a new order on every load; more notes go against type than with it.

Rule 30: written things are blank or shut: the wedding card, the shut register, the ruled list with no marks, the calendar's empty grid, sealed plain envelopes, the plain cake box, and the tempo with its plate hidden behind chairs.

Rules 32 and 33: no card person is painted; every decision backdrop is people-free; outcome pictures show the event, never who was picked. Mama ji and Nani are never face-on inside the look (Nani only in the present-day album), and the list at 5.26 reuses the 5.04 reference.

Rules 3, 4, 12 and 48: the wedding is told as logistics only, with no ritual, prayer, religious symbol, brand, famous person or community place named. The bride and groom are never drawn or named, and no festival is named. There are no city prices and no domestic help at the centre (only a hired cook, caterer and canopy man). Everyone on the cards is 28 to 45, with no child on a card.
Rule 35: one shout in the chapter (5.03); every narration box gives only time and place; sound words are single.

Rule 22: judging notes come only from named voices with face chips, a woman's (Mami) and a man's (Mama ji). Each keeps one voice across both halves of its twin, and none speaks of women or men in general.

Rules 42, 44, 45 and 46: the outcome comes after the last pick in three beats: the event with its stamp, the stamped list, and Mama ji's warm line for the band with your fixed reply. It names nobody and never says right, wrong or well done. The fixed lines never say where the tins were or whose account was right. Bars sit at or below each equal two; the cards that miss a bar are 3 women and 3 men, counting each card; the 'matters' twin has a fixed result; all three stamp times can happen.

Rules 49 to 52 and owner answers 2 to 4: you are the grown-up child of the house, handed the job list; the chapter is one strip with each decision a stop; Jadugar is only the look of a present-day December wedding, in calendar order. There are 8 decisions in 4 twins (plain, hard, matters, plain), each pair four decisions apart, with the story clock on every decision and the December ring filling by decision. Four kinds appear, only one new: Believe, first met in its home world with the moving hand, completing all seven across the take. The album opens on a tap and leads to the five reading cards as built.

Rules 62 and 63, on the proposed caps. No story beat is over 20 counted words, and only 5.01 has more than three pieces (marked). No spoken line is over 10 (5.27 at most 4 English and 6 Hindi a band) and no narration over 12.
