verdicts.reasons:
Judged on the players only, reading all five chapters on a phone as each of the six players would.

WHAT WORKS, and it is the best spine Retake has had:
- The opening places you inside 40 words (1.01 to 1.06): Nani's "Everyone comes", Mummy's free calendar from the shop, "Everyone calls you anyway" and the pen.
- Nobody ever says your age. Being the grown-up child everyone phones works for Mr Natarajan the way the shaadi demo did.
- One chapter leads to the next all year: the wet step (1.40), the ward (2.02), the July pencil circle, the cracked drain (3.28), the drain as the cup's stake (4.03), Nani's card (4.28), and the cake box (2.33) paid off at 5.28 and 5.29.
- The train, the ward and the wedding pass "lived it or watched it at home" for all six.
- Outcomes are warm in every band. There are no rituals, festivals or brands.
- The household lines sound like people you know: "9:40, not 9:45", "My lane is here. Use them.", "Sixty guests? Make it seventy!"

WHY IT SITS BELOW DADI'S CALENDAR'S 7. Seeing the whole take shows four things the three sample decisions hid:
1. There are almost no people in the panels. Only 13 of 117 story beats show a face, and 3 of those are in the present-day opening and album. About 50 beats are people-free, and every lead-in is the asker's back in the left third. Characters talk to each other about once a chapter (2.03, 3.02, 5.03). So each chapter goes clock, back, cards, empty settled plate, eight times. "Fourteen people, ten berths" never pays off after D1.
2. Several asks are things nobody in your place would really be asked (rule 5).
3. The cards read as an NGO poster, and the same kinds of people always come last.
4. Many smaller stumbles:
   - The target lists read like spreadsheet rules (1.11, 2.04, 5.04). In chapters 1, 2 and 5 a player cannot see why the picks change the stamp: why do the trains missed by the first auto's riders decide when you reach Nani's door?
   - Title cards promise a plot the story never tells. 2.01's "a quarrel over a house" comes right after Nani's fall, and 5.01's "talk of a dowry" sits on the family's own wedding.
   - Chapter 4 uses gully cricket words a newcomer may not know (slips, off-spin, 4.09 and 4.11). Its mixed lane side, 18 to 60, is one the tailor and the banking agent have watched but not played.
   - "Slips" means fielders in chapter 4 and counting mistakes in chapter 5.
   - Kader "Moved back here in June" (4.07) but "Has lived here for forty years" (4.16).
   - "Tonight, you're in charge" appears word for word at 1.10 and 2.04.
   - In 5.03 it is unclear who Mami's "you" is.
   - You tell elders "पहले सब पानी पियो" (4.14), which is curt.
   - The Hinglish mode is still undecided, so Hindi-first players may meet the opening in English.
   - Chapter 3, hiring hands for the family shop, is the one event Shruti, Mr Natarajan and Farida may not have lived.
   - Chapter 5's tent over the lane and brass band lean north Indian.
   - Gujarati cousins in chapter 1 and Bengali relatives in chapter 5, both on Mummy's side, read as token names, not one family.
problems: THE STRIP CARRIES A CLOCK, NOT PEOPLE. Every lead-in is the asker's back in the left third: Papa at 1.13, 1.19, 1.22, 1.25, 1.31 and 1.34; Nani at 2.06, 2.09, 2.12, 2.18, 2.21 and 2.24; Mummy at 3.06, 3.11, 3.16 and 3.21; Mama ji at 5.06, 5.08, 5.11, 5.14, 5.16, 5.18, 5.21 and 5.23. Almost every 'it happened' beat is an empty set with a sound (1.15 to 1.36, 2.08 to 2.29, 3.08 to 3.25, 4.08 to 4.23). Only 10 story beats inside the chapter looks show a face (1.09, 2.03, 2.17, 3.02, 3.28, 4.03, 4.06, 4.15, 5.03, 5.04). The household never talks to each other in chapter 1's train scenes; the only face there is Mausi's shout at 1.09. The owner asked for characters who talk to each other with you among them. That happens only in the opening, so the household is a face chip and a back, and Sunita, who plays from pictures, gets lead-in, cards, empty plate, eight times a chapter.

ASKS NOBODY IN YOUR PLACE WOULD MAKE (rule 5), so the 'is this my life' test fails at the decision itself. A family shop hands the cash drawer (3.24) and the 6 am opening keys (3.14) to applicants hired that week while Mummy and you stand at the counter. Nani's spare house key (2.10) and her purse during the X-ray (2.22) go to neighbours while you, her grandchild, and Mausa ji are at the bed. Papa sends one cousin alone to another coach at 11 pm (1.20). A woman alone in a coach at night means something different in most Indian homes, so Ravi and Farida answer from protectiveness, not fairness, and the twin (1.32, a warm bench in a busy waiting room) does not carry that weight. On top of this, the title cards announce the hard topic as if it will happen in the story ('a quarrel over a house' at 2.01, straight after Nani's fall; 'talk of a dowry' at 5.01 on the family's own wedding; 'a report of being followed' at 1.07 for this train). It then turns up only as one card about someone's past.

THE CARDS READ AS A POSTER AND A PECKING ORDER. Against-type jobs are on nearly every card and repeat from chapter to chapter: women drive tempos (1.17, 4.18, 5.15) and coach or play kabaddi (1.35, 3.07, 4.22); men run tiffin services (1.23, 2.16, 3.12) and stitch uniforms (2.10, 3.07). One family's cousins look like an NGO casting call, which is what makes Shruti ('spot the sexist') and Ravi ('NGO lecture') quit. And across the take the weakest cards are the community-marked, the old, the widowed and the bereaved. In chapter 1 Hetal and Mehul sit lowest six times (1.17, 1.29, 1.32, 1.35). In chapter 2 Nagsen, Yasmin and Mumtaz are the weakest in 5 of 7 decisions (2.07, 2.10, 2.16, 2.22, 2.25). Nagsen is a name many Ambedkarite Buddhist families use, so it may read as caste-marked, not only Marathi; a reader from that community should check. In chapter 3 Francis is weakest at 3.19 to 3.24 and the widow Kusum at 3.07, 3.09, 3.14 and 3.17. In chapter 4 Zarina and Kader sit at the foot of 4.13. In chapter 5 Lalit, who 'lost his father to a fever in March', is weakest at 5.07 to 5.17. The writers marked each case alone; seen together it is the pattern that makes Farida and Meena quit, and the screenshot the hostile screenshotter (anti-persona A2) wants.
verdicts.fix: Put the household back into the panels. Answer options Q11 by painting each chapter's asker face-on in that chapter's look from one reference portrait. That is five paintings, each with the close-up check for painted dots and lightened skin; the name tag and face chip already on every bubble cover face drift. Then rewrite each scene's lead-in as a short exchange between the asker and the chapter voice that turns to you. For example, at 1.13 Mausi says 'Lower berth for me, obviously' and Papa says 'Two lower berths. Your call.', which also pays off 'fourteen people, ten berths'. Keep people-free 'it happened' panels only at a change of place, as rule 50 already says. Twin lead-ins can still match: the same two figures, the same mood, word counts within 2. No bubble words change on the cards, so the measure is untouched. This one change gives every player faces to know, a strip that tells a story between the stops, and the owner's 'characters talk to each other, you are one of them' inside the chapters, not just in the opening.

verdicts.reasons:
Measure only, judged on all 40 written decisions (I re-tabulated every card's numbers from chapter-1.json to chapter-5.json).

What holds up. Outcomes are clean. Every chapter tried every answer: swapping the equal two, always picking the woman and always picking the man all end the same. Every bar sits at or below the pair. Cards that miss a bar are as often women as men (chapter 1: 2 and 2; chapter 5: 3 and 3). Each chapter has one hard topic, on one card, never in a bubble. The household never sits on a card. Each twin keeps one asker and one remark voice, which fixes the first samples' worst tell. Most number keys suit their task: hours on feet and hours slept for berths and cots, runs and matches for batting, years in shop work and days late for the counter. Rank, team and split decisions straddle the cut properly (rule 14). Chapter 2's same-sex sibling quarrels show real care on rule 28, and chapter 4's hard twin (a separation, against slip and bowling places) is the cleanest in the take. All five areas are present. But chapter 1's 'Safety and justice' reading is fed mostly by berths, plates, cash and autos, not by safety.

What sinks it is the question 'is the bias too easy to spot?' Yes, and from chapter 1.
1. In 38 of 40 decisions the equal two are the only two cards with matching numbers. The writers prove that rule 15 cannot hold with 10-person circles and fixed numbers per set.
2. In 18 decisions (every pick one and believe) the equal two sit together at the top, beating every other card on both numbers. The choice is plainly 'which of these two identical people'. Four of the five hard twins (chapters 1, 2, 3 and 5) use this shape, and their topic is also named on the title card and flagged by the plain question box.
3. In chapter 5 the two numbers never disagree, so every screen is a strict ladder.
4. The heavy decoy facts sit on beaten or bottom cards, and chapter 4's hard decisions have none.
5. Some loaded words read as sexist on sight: 'drama queen', 'bossy', 'too emotional', 'too shy'.
6. The matters twins come back as near-copies with the gender flipped. Chapter 1's 'battery dead, one charged phone' returns at 2:30 am with a matched painting, so a player learns how twins work by decision 6.

Second, several twins do not return cleanly, because the nudge bears on the task in one half and not the other. Third, a few honours are handed out by numbers no family would use, and four spend-checks decisions let a player skip the equal two altogether.

For calibration, the first-round judges gave Dadi's Calendar 7 and Five Ordinary Days 5 from samples. On the whole written take the blend scores 5: the outcomes are sound, but the reading can be seen through.
problems: THE PAIR IS GIVEN AWAY BY THE NUMBERS. In 38 of 40 decisions the equal two are the only two cards with matching numbers. The two exceptions, 3.14 and 3.24, add the same two men (Rohit and Anthony, 10 and 1) below the pair both times, and only in the hard decisions. In all 18 pick-one and believe decisions (1.17, 1.20, 1.29, 1.32, 2.10, 2.13, 2.22, 2.25, 3.09, 3.14, 3.19, 3.24, 4.13, 4.22, 5.09, 5.12, 5.19, 5.22) the two sit together at the top, beating every other card on both numbers. Four of the five hard twins use this shape (1.20/1.32, 2.10/2.22, 3.14/3.24, 5.09/5.19), on top of the title card naming the topic and the plain question box. Chapter 5's numbers never disagree, so every screen is a ladder (5.07 to 5.24). The heavy decoy facts sit only on beaten or bottom cards (1.32 Vivek, 3.14 Kusum, 5.09 Lalit, 5.19 Rekha), and the hard decisions 4.11 and 4.20 have none. The same person is bottom card again and again (Lalit in 5.07 to 5.12, Kusum in 3.07 to 3.17, Francis in 3.19 to 3.24, Nagsen in ch2), so players learn to skip them. Matters twins return as near-copies with the gender flipped, the 'one charged phone' at 1.16/1.17 coming back at 1.28/1.29 and the 'one a keeper' question at 4.09 coming back at 4.18, so the twin mechanism shows by chapter 1's decision 6. Some loaded words read as sexist on sight: 'drama queen' (4.16), 'bossy' (3.07), 'too emotional' (4.13), 'too shy' (1.23).

TWIN HALVES THAT DO NOT MEAN THE SAME. Plain twins change meaning, not just words, so the nudge bears on the task in one half only. At 3.12 the woman is 'chatty', which has nothing to do with drying stock on a roof; at 3.22 the man is 'careless with small things', a real reason to keep him off sorting new stock, so a careful player is read as leaning towards women. Also 3.07 'bossy' against 3.17 'quick to anger' at a customer counter, and 4.13 'emotional' against 4.22 'hot-headed' for an umpire. Hard twins: at 1.20 being followed bears on moving alone to another coach at 11 pm (a safety call either way), while at 1.32 it is a warm waiting-room bench; 'last trip' is also more recent than 'once'. At 5.09/5.19 'refused a scooter demand' is itself a reason to trust someone with the gift register or the jewellery room, so the hard twin works as a second matters twin and reads integrity, not a lean. At 2.10/2.22 a quarrel over a family home bears more on keeping Nani's house key than on holding her purse.

DECISIONS THAT CAN DODGE THE PAIR, OR HAVE NO BELIEVABLE REASON TO CHOOSE. 2.16 and 2.28 ('at least one') and 5.07 and 5.17 ('one person may carry both') let a player give everything to the single card that beats everyone (Rajan, Nagsen, Sarla, Naresh). Two whole twins (chapter 2's D and chapter 5's A) can then return no reading, and the targets reward giving fewer. Honours are decided by numbers no family would use: the seat beside Nani at 5.15 and carrying her cake at 5.24 by 'weddings helped at' and 'counting slips', and the first auto at 1.35 by 'night trips' and 'trains missed', a target nobody can explain. At 2.19 (6 am) the cards still show the 9 pm slip's 'slept last night'. Roles that may not read the same for a woman and a man, for readers to check: the jewellery-room key (5.19), a man sitting overnight at an elderly woman's ward bed (2.07), moving alone to another coach at night (1.20), and a mixed lane-cricket side under last-over pressure (4.13).
verdicts.fix: Rebuild each chapter's number design so the equal two are neither the only tie nor two identical cards at the top. Every chapter's solver hit the same limit: with 10 people and fixed numbers per set, the two people left over in each set are always one woman and one man, so no two women or two men can tie. Grow each circle to 12 so each set leaves two spare women and two spare men, or let numbers be set per decision. Then put a tie between two women or two men on most screens, beside or above the pair. Keep pick one and believe for the matters twins only, where following the reason both times is fair. Recast the hard twin and the plain twins as rank, team, batting order or split decisions that straddle the cut, as chapter 4's hard twin already does at 4.11/4.20. Then re-run each chapter's outcome checks, and give every competing card, not just the bottom one, a chance to carry a heavy decoy fact.

verdicts.reasons:
MAKING IT, judged on the whole written take, checked against the repo and the art folder.

FITS WHAT IS BUILT (the strong side):
- All seven decision kinds the blend uses already exist in src/take/steps and data.ts: pick, believe (pick with teller), checks, rank, team, order, split. Team sizes such as 2 of 5 and Split with 3 jobs are only settings.
- The worlds keep today's world-to-area pairs, and each world's big moment (Lugdi's reprint, Station's flaps, Jadugar's cloth, Cricket's 'decision pending', Rukavat's card) is already a signature move in DESIGN.md:551.
- The present-day pages can use the painter's existing STYLE['now'] (cutscenes.py:103), so no sixth style is needed.
- Faces are handled the way the painter needs. The household is only ever painted in today's style, and inside a chapter's look it is seen from behind or heard off the panel, with a face chip. Card people appear in one chapter only.
- 42 of the 50 card people already have portraits in their chapter's look (pulp-, sunday-, enamel-, cricket-face-, jadugar-*.webp). Chapters 1 and 2 need no new card face at all, and the painted ages match.
- Every painting brief follows the bubble spec's composition rules (heads 30 to 45% down, first speaker on the left, a calm space named). Each beat stays within 3 pieces of text, and there is at most one shout a chapter.
- Word counts stay under the caps in all five chapters.

WHAT IT COSTS (the weak side):
1. Paintings. The take is 162 beats and about 153 different paintings. The scroll design budgeted about 18 a chapter (about 90); the app has 69 today. The extra comes from four things:
   - every one of the 40 decisions gets its own people-free backdrop, each also needing a wide laptop version;
   - every decision gets its own lead-in;
   - there are 35 'it happened' panels, where rule 50 allows one only at a change of place;
   - the kitchen calendar is repainted about nine times.
   Counting about 30 portraits, that is roughly 220 images. Even at the strip's 3 to 6 tries each, that is 600 to 1,300 tries for the owner's eye check. Chapter 1 alone is 41 beats. With 122 story beats at about 4 seconds each on top of 40 decisions, the take runs to about 25 minutes against 20.
2. Painted letters. Many briefs ask for exactly the subjects where B4 found 27 of 69 panels with letters: blank calendar grids, clocks 'with hands only', blank scoreboard slates, plain number plates, blank name boards and a blank split-flap board. Several looks are lettered by nature (pulp covers, railway posters, playbills, scoreboards).
3. Hindi and Hinglish.
   - Writers used the 'sign' type for interface text (labels, settled plates, buttons, the title card, progress), and in Hinglish mode the spec puts Hindi on every sign (DESIGN.md:449).
   - In the default mode, the lists of targets and the stamped lists would therefore show Hindi beside English card keys.
   - No Hinglish line is written at all (rulebook Q6), and lines are English and Hindi pairs only.
   - The opening and story beats sit close to the caps (chapter 5's Hindi is at 120 of 120 counting the title card), so there is no room left for Hinglish or for fixes.
4. Screens. 18 of the 40 decisions show five cards with a note on every card, twice today's 9, on a 360 x 640 phone in Hindi (still waiting on Q16).
5. Faces that will drift. Chapter voices are painted face-on several times in one look: Captain sahab 4.03, 4.06 and 4.15; Mausa ji 2.03 and 2.17; Masterji 3.02 and 3.28; Mami 5.03 and 5.04. Each also needs a face-chip portrait. Present-day faces are repainted too (Mummy 1.02, 1.03, 1.05; Nani 1.03, 5.29). Name tags on every bubble are the backstop.
6. New code beyond the strip's 7 to 8 days:
   - the calendar progress rings laid over painted grids;
   - the story clock in the top bar;
   - a face chip on each judging note;
   - an outcome engine that handles counts with varying totals (chapter 2's {k}/{n}), a sum (chapter 4's openers' runs) and line-ups by band;
   - a new type for interface text, separate from sign;
   - a third text column once Hinglish is defined.
7. Data. The five chapter files use five different layouts: kind strings, speaker ids ('game', 'the game', '-', 'Narration'), buttons buried in prose, and role and age inside chapter 5's note strings. Five separate checkers read rule 17 differently. None of this can feed app_content.py without a normalising pass and one shared exporter check.
8. Results lines. The bible says the results screen needs no change, but some area lines no longer fit. Jadugar's 'believed when the man tells it' now sits on a chapter whose Believe pair is the fixed 'matters' twin.

FASTEST PATH TO ONE PLAYABLE CHAPTER: chapter 1.
- It opens the take and carries the blend's main bets: your phone, the household page, the calendar, the list of targets and the stamp.
- Its kinds (Rank, Pick one, Pick a team 2 of 5) need no code, all ten cousins already have pulp portraits at the right ages, and the Lugdi reprint exists.
- Trim it first: keep the 'it happened' panels only at the three changes of place (1.24, 1.30, 1.36); paint the coach bay, the long-halt platform and Nani's station once each as both gate and laptop backdrops; paint the calendar once. That takes it from 39 to about 22 paintings.
- Then: the parts sheet (about 2 days, owner's yes); the strip and gates inline (2); panels and bubbles with the placement page (3 to 4); the household and circle pages, the top-bar clock and calendar rings (1); chapter 1's outcome table, with two count targets and three stamps (1); normalising chapter-1.json into the script format and moving ch1tools into story_take.py refusals (1 to 1.5); one overnight heavyq run of about 2 hours, the owner's eye pass and the text check; about an hour of bubble placement; then play it from a first run.
- That is about 10 to 12 working days after the parts-sheet yes.
- Chapter 4 is cheaper to paint (about 23 paintings with its built-in reuse, 9 of 10 faces exist), but it needs the batting-order change and a new target type, and it does not test the opening.
problems:
PAINTING VOLUME, about double the scroll design's budget. The causes:
- Every stop gets its own people-free gate backdrop (all 40 decision beats, 1.14 to 5.24), each also needing a wide version.
- Every stop gets its own lead-in, and 1.28 repaints 1.16 rather than reusing it.
- There are 35 'it happened' panels: 1.15, 1.18, 1.21, 1.27, 1.33; 2.08, 2.11, 2.20, 2.23, 2.26, 2.29; 3.08 to 3.25; 4.08 to 4.23. Rule 50 allows one only at a change of place, and the writers' notes for chapters 2 and 3 admit the brief added them.
- The calendar is repainted at 1.02, 1.03, 1.04, 1.06, 2.34, 3.29, 4.02, 5.02 and 5.30.
Result: about 153 different paintings (39 in chapter 1 alone) plus about 40 wide versions and about 30 portraits. That is roughly 220 images and 600 to 1,300 tries for the owner's eye check, against about 90 budgeted and 69 today. Play time comes to about 25 minutes against 20.

PAINTED LETTERS AND THE TEXT LAYER.
- Letter-prone briefs, the same kinds of objects where B4 found letters: blank calendar grids (1.02, 1.04, 1.06, 2.34, 3.29, 5.02, 5.30), clocks 'with hands only' (1.32, 2.02, 2.06, 2.08), blank scoreboard slates (4.08, 4.12, 4.24), plain number plates (1.34, 2.27, 2.29, 3.09, 3.10) and blank name boards (1.30, 2.01, 2.21, 3.26's split-flap board). Several of the looks themselves are lettered genres.
- Text typed as 'sign': 1.03's labels, the settled plates 1.15 to 1.36, 1.07, 1.41's buttons, 2.34 and 4.08 'Order ✓'.
- In Hinglish, the default, the spec letters every sign in Hindi (DESIGN.md:449). The lists of targets (1.11, 2.04, 3.04, 4.04, 5.04) and the stamped lists (1.38, 2.31, 3.27, 4.25, 5.26) would then show Hindi beside English card keys, which breaks 'targets in the same words as the card numbers'.
- No Hinglish line is written anywhere (rulebook Q6), and the data holds only English and Hindi pairs.

NOT BUILDABLE AS WRITTEN, AND PORTRAITS THAT DO NOT FIT.
- Batting order: 4.07 and 4.16 ask for the order and the captain on one card as one decision, with two balloons at the fixed question place. Today they are two steps and two decisions (cricket-1 and cricket-2). The chapter's own notes say the captain stage feeds nothing and breaks rule 14.
- Two checks on one person: 5.07 and 5.17 let one person carry both envelopes or both keys, but Pick.tsx gives one check per card.
- Button label: 2.16 and 2.28 need 'Give at least one', but Pick.tsx:35 fixes the label as 'Take up at least one'.
- Chapter 5 portraits: writer note 3 says the four faces whose ages change are not yet painted, but Dolly and Tapan already are. jadugar-dolly is painted at 41 in a velvet stage jacket (5.07, 5.22, 5.24 need 33), and jadugar-tapan at 37 (5.12, 5.24 need 40). Sarla wears a sequinned stage blouse, Lalit a bow tie and satin waistcoat, and Shampa has a bindi.
- Chapter 3 portraits: the Station faces wear railway uniforms (Annamma, Rohit, and Francis 'with shoulder straps'), so in 3.07 to 3.24 they read as railway staff, not people answering Mummy's notice. Chapter 5 needs about 8 repaints, not 2, and chapter 3 another 3 or so on top of its 5 new faces.
- Data: the five chapter files use five different layouts, so none can be exported without a normalising pass and one shared checker.
verdicts.fix:
Paint by scene, not by stop, and make the exporter enforce it.
- Paint each place once, people-free, in portrait and wide. Use it as the laptop backdrop and as the gate backdrop for every stop in that place.
- Where the two halves of a twin happen in the same place, they share one lead-in painting and change only the clock and the words. Chapter 4 already does this at 4.08/4.17, 4.10/4.19, 4.12/4.21, which makes rule 37's 'matching lead-ins' true by construction.
- Keep 'it happened' panels only at a change of place or day, as rule 50 and chapter 5 already do.
- Paint the calendar, Papa's list, Nani's file, Mummy's paper, Tinku's sheet and Mami's card once each, as reused props with one set of live-text corners.
- Cap a chapter at about 18 to 20 different paintings in the exporter (story_take.py), alongside its word caps.
This cuts the take from about 153 to about 90 paintings and from about 220 to about 130 images. It also roughly halves the owner's eye check and the number of letter-prone surfaces, brings play time back near 20 minutes, and makes chapter 1 (about 22 paintings, no new kinds, all ten faces already painted) playable in about 10 to 12 days after the parts-sheet yes.
Do the two cheap fixes in the same pass: give interface text and the lists of targets their own type that follows the chosen language, not 'sign'; and drop the captain stage (4.07, 4.16) and the two-checks-on-one-person rule (5.07, 5.17) rather than adding code for them.

problems.beats: Take-wide; every title card (1.07, 2.01, 3.01, 4.01, 5.01) says 'About 4 minutes'
problems.problem: The take is about 50% longer than the 20 minutes it is meant to run. It has 162 beats: 40 decision stops and 122 story beats, against about 6 pictures a chapter today. The scroll design's own method (3 to 4 s for each extra panel) already gives 25 to 26 minutes, and the judges called that method low. Add 279 bubbles, 178 cards with about 1,110 English and 1,250 Hindi counted note words, and seven first-time kinds that each show a moving hand: a newcomer more likely needs 28 to 32 minutes, and longer in Hindi. Within a chapter, 8 stops at 25 to 30 s each already take 3.5 to 4 minutes before its roughly 24 story beats, so each chapter runs about 5 to 6 minutes. No tap ceiling has been set (rule 50).
problems.fix: Time chapter 1 with five newcomers before writing more, and set the tap ceiling from that timing (rule 50). Cheapest cut: keep 'it happened' beats only at a change of place, as the bible and chapter 5 do. That drops about 20 beats in chapters 1 to 4. Let the settled plate carry the job word, and keep one lead-in per scene. Then print the chapter time the playtest measures instead of 'About 4 minutes'.

problems.problem: In chapter 4, players are in two matches at once. The final starts at 2:30 (D5, toss 2:40). Who stands?' | '4:30 के मैच को अंपायर चाहिए। किसे भेजें?' Paint the 4.18 and 4.22 backdrops as the other pitch set up and empty. The same loaded remarks come back in several chapters (rule 6: no nudge wording used twice):

verdicts.totals:
The take has 5 chapters and 162 beats: 40 decision stops and 122 story beats (17 opening or hand-over beats, 5 title cards, 40 lead-ins and circle pages, 35 'it happened' beats, 25 closing beats including 2 album beats). There are 279 bubbles and 178 cards. Each beat is one painting; about 11 reuse an earlier painting, so about 150 new paintings, roughly double the scroll design's 15 to 18 a chapter.

Counted words (no names or numbers, one outcome band):
- Story beats: about 760 English and 785 Hindi.
- Title cards: 85 and 92.
- Opening: 43 and 50.
- Decision questions: 262 and 258.
- Card notes: 1,112 and 1,253.
- In all, about 2,260 English and 2,440 Hindi counted words on screen, before keys, buttons, the album and the five reading cards.

Playing time: about 25 to 26 minutes by the scroll design's own method, and more likely 28 to 32 for a newcomer, longer in Hindi, against about 20. That is about 5 to 6 minutes a chapter against the 'About 4 minutes' every title card promises, and at least 280 taps.

- Household ages and roles hold throughout: Nani 80, Mummy 52, Papa 56, Tinku 21, Mama ji 'Mummy's brother'.
- Askers are 3 women and 2 men; voices are 5 and 5.
- Every chapter's targets compute, and all three bands are reachable.
- The ending-to-opening chain holds from 1 to 2 (the wet step), 2 to 3 (July) and 3 to 4 (the drain); 4 to 5 holds but repeats the card.
- No Hindi line by or to the player marks gender.
